en: Homage to that Self of All, in whom is everything, from whom is everything, who is everything, who is everywhere, and who is eternally composed of everything. (Rasāyana 1.1)
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, adorned with various jewels, filled with diverse trees and creepers, and free from hidden attachments. (Ras 1.2)
Having bowed her head to the God of gods, the blue-throated, three-eyed one who was seated comfortably, the Goddess Pārvatī questioned him. (Ras 1.3)
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, O Kāla, burner of the limbs of Kāma, destroyer of Kulakaula, Mahākaula, Siddhakaula, and the rest! (Ras 1.4)
Through your grace, everything has been heard and fully mastered;
if I am worthy of your favor, and if I am dear to you. (Ras 1.5)
"O Lord, this liberation while living has been indicated in all the tantras, yet it has not been further elucidated; you should tell me, what is its nature? (Rasāyana 1.6)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! Excellent, O daughter of the mountain!
Well asked by you, O Goddess, out of a desire for the welfare of devotees. (Rasārṇava 1.7)

O Great Goddess, the realization of identity with Śiva while possessing a body that is free from old age and death—this is liberation while living (jīvanmukti), which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (Ras 1.8)
And that liberation which is found in alms-food is a liberation devoid of meaning;
for when the food has fallen, O Goddess, even a donkey is liberated. (Ras 1.9)
O Mother of the Gaṇas, if liberation occurs through the agitation of the *bhaga*, why do donkeys, goats, and bulls not attain liberation? Ras_1.10 //
Therefore, one should protect the *piṇḍa* with juices and elixirs (*rasāyana*), provided that there is liberation through the consumption of semen, urine, and feces. (Ras 1.11)
O Great Goddess, why were those born as dogs and pigs not liberated?
For even in the Six Darśanas, liberation is shown to occur at the falling away of the body. (Ras 1.12)
O Goddess, although that [reality] is not perceived directly like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, I shall describe its true nature to you, even though it is unspeakable. (Rasāyana 1.13)
One who is devoid of sin and performs the sacrifice of mantra should never maintain a physical body (*piṇḍa*);
for even among the gods, O Goddess of Gods, the maintenance of a physical body is difficult to attain. (Ras_1.14)
How much more so for humans dwelling upon the surface of the earth?
When the Dharma has perished, where is the Dharma? When the Dharma has perished, where is ritual action?
If action is lost, whence is yoga? If yoga is lost, whence is spiritual progress? If spiritual progress is lost, whence is liberation? If liberation is lost, there is nothing at all. (Ras 1.16)
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, I have heard the nature of liberation while living;
if you have compassion for me, tell me the means to attain it."
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess of the gods, the maintenance of the physical body is attained through the yoga of action (*karmayoga*).
This *karmayoga* is considered to be twofold: mercury (*rasa*) and breath (*pavana*). (Rasārṇava 1.18)
When swooned, O Bhairavī, the mercury removes disease; when dead, it restores life by itself; when bound, it grants the power of moving through the sky—so too does the vital air. Ras 1.19.
O Goddess of the gods, liberation comes from knowledge; knowledge arises from the practice of breath-retention (pavanadhāraṇa).
O Goddess, where the physical body (piṇḍa) is stable, there the mercury (rasa) becomes sovereign through that stability. (Rasārṇava 1.20)
O Goddess, through the application of the essence (*rasa*), a body free from old age and death is soon produced, just as meditative absorption is attained by the mind. (Ras 1.21)
O Goddess, he who consumes the *mṛtasūtaka* truly attains knowledge preceded by higher realization (*vijñāna*), and his mantras become efficacious. (Rasārṇava 1.22)
As long as there is no descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and as long as there is no severing of the bonds (*pāśa*), how could the realization regarding death and birth arise in him? (Ras 1.23)

For those who are constantly addicted to liquor and meat, and who take pleasure in the female and male organs, it is extremely difficult for those of ruined intellect to attain knowledge of the true essence. (Rasāyana 1.24)
O Goddess, for those devoid of noble lineage and instruction, who do not desire the true vision, the elixir is not accomplished; they drink from a mirage. (Rasāyana 1.25)
"I consider him who eats beef and drinks the nectar of the gods (amaravāruṇī) to be of noble birth and a connoisseur of flavors; others are base. — Rasārṇava 1.26.
The embryo is not for the sake of mere tradition; the embryo is prescribed as the "rasa" (essence).
Through that, one attains accomplishment; there is no accomplishment without the "sūtaka" (birth-fluid/elixir). (Rasāyana 1.27)
As long as one does not consume the seed of Hara—the mercury (pārada) essence—how can there be liberation for him, and how can there be the maintenance of the physical body? (Rasāyana 1.28)
Delighting in liquor and meat, their wisdom deluded by the māyā of Śiva, they prattle: "We are liberated; we shall go to the abode of Śiva. (Ras 1.29)

O Goddess of Gods, those of dull intellect, devoid of desire for the yoga of sustaining the *piṇḍa*, believe that the entire world of moving and non-moving things is colored by fragmentary knowledge. Ras_1.30.
O beloved, practice constantly that knowledge of mercury by which the state of moving through the sky and the state of Śiva are attained within one's own body. (Rasārṇava 1.31)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the Gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, I wish to hear about the descent of Rasendra and its majesty; O Lord of Devas, you should speak of it according to the truth. (Ras 1.32)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Well asked, O highly fortunate one, by you! This meditation, which bestows grace and benefits the worlds, is more secret than the most secret. (Rasāyana 1.33)
You are the mother of all beings, and I am the eternal father;
O Goddess, that which is the essence of the two, born from the great sexual union— // Ras_1.34 //

O Goddess, mercury (pārada) is celebrated as the Great Radiance (mahaḥ) because it arises from its own will; and it is called pārada because it is employed for the sake of others by the most excellent practitioners. (Ras 1.35)
"O Goddess, this Sūta is equal to me, born from my very own body;
since he is the essence (rasa) of my body, he is therefore called Rasa. (Ras 1.36)
From seeing it, from touching it, from consuming it, and even from remembering it, as well as from worshipping it and giving it away, a sixfold fruit is observed. (Ras 1.37)
Whatever merit is gained from seeing the Kedāra and other such lingas on earth, that same merit is obtained from the sight of the mercury. (Rasāyana 1.38)
The essence contained within sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron, when intensified, serves for the worship of Śiva in order to achieve the presence of Śiva. (Ras 1.39)
O Supreme Goddess, by consuming this elixir, one destroys the three types of sin;
likewise, it destroys the three types of suffering and the diseases arising from the three humors. (Rasāyana 1.40)

O Maheśvarī, that which is difficult to attain is obtained by those perfected in Brahman: the supreme state residing within the pericarp of the sky of the heart, [the state] of mercury (rasendra). (Ras_1.41)
By remembering [this], one is immediately liberated from sins accumulated over many lifetimes. (Ras 1.42)

Whatever fruit is obtained from the perfect worship of thousands of self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅgas, that fruit shall be multiplied ten millionfold by the worship of a mercury-liṅga (rasaliṅga). (Ras 1.43)

The science of alchemy (khagavāda) is the lowest; the science of minerals (vilavāda) is middling; the science of mantras (mantravāda) is superior; and the science of elixirs (rasavāda) is the most excellent. (Rasāyana 1.44)
Those who, despite their thorough knowledge of mantra and tantra, disparage the application of mercury, all go to hell after having destroyed their accumulation of merit. (Rasāyana 1.45)

The science of alchemy (rasavidyā) is the supreme knowledge, exceedingly difficult to find even in the three worlds; since it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, it should therefore be imparted by those endowed with virtue. (Ras 1.46)
One person says "it exists," while another says "it does not exist";
however, success belongs to the believer, and for him it is accomplished on this earth. (Ras 1.47)
For one who, through a nihilistic disposition, says "it does not exist, it does not exist," there is no accomplishment regarding what is dear, even in hundreds of millions of births. (Ras 1.48)
Even one who is a sinner, such as a reviler of the tongue, becomes liberated through the knowledge of Brahman;
yet I shall not be his savior even in hundreds of millions of births.
O Goddess, this person is born as a dog for as long as a thousand births;
due to [the consumption of] mercury (rasa), he is born as a cat for three million births, as a donkey for a hundred thousand births, and as a crow for a hundred thousand births. (Rasāyana 1.50)
The sinner who reviles the tongue becomes a worm for a hundred thousand births, a cock for a hundred thousand births, and a vulture for a hundred thousand births. (Ras 1.51)
Whoever engages in conversation or physical contact with those who revile the tongue shall be tormented by suffering for as many as a thousand lifetimes. (Ras 1.52)
In terms of taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation, mercury (sūtaka) is like nectar;
therefore, O beloved, mercury removes birth, old age, and disease. (Rasārṇava 1.53)
One should first propitiate the guru with a purified inner self;
for when the guru is satisfied, the Marīcis bestow the oral tradition.
The fool-minded person who performs ritual action without service to the guru attains fruitless action, just like wealth acquired in a dream. (Ras 1.55)
Whoever performs the visible rite gains profit at every step;
however, O beloved, one should cause the discourse on mercury to be performed only when the Guru is pleased. (Rasārṇava 1.56)
This instruction on the means of accomplishment bestows both enjoyment and liberation upon both [practitioners];
this great tantra, the *Rasārṇava*, is exceedingly difficult to obtain. (Ras 1.57)
That which is secret should be obtained through the grace of the Guru for the sake of attaining the fruit;
having acquired the practices of alchemy here, one should not practice egoism. (Rasāyana 1.58)
Having been authorized by the guru and having received the command for the *rasāṅkuśī*,
one should assume the form of Bhairavī and accomplish *Rasabhairava*.
Thus has the origin of mercury and its majesty been described, O Sovereign of the Gods.
Tell me that, O Goddess of Devas; what else do you wish to hear? (Rasārṇava 1.60)
The Second Chapter: [The Procedure for Initiation].
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, tell me, how may one become a teacher of the instruction on mercury?"
And how, O Lord, does a disciple become intent upon the practice of alchemy? (Rasāyana 2.1)
The illustrious Bhairava said: He who is free from desire, devoid of ego, and abandoned by greed and illusion;
who is constantly devoted to the path of Kula and intent upon the worship of the Guru. (Rasārṇava 2.2)
Self-controlled, knowledgeable in instructing disciples, capable, free from envy, knower of the Dharma, truthful in speech, skillful, virtuous, endowed with good qualities, and pure. (Ras 2.3)
He is a knower of many treatises on alchemy (*rasa*), skilled in the pavilion of mercury,
and conversant with the procedures for the initiation into mercury, as well as with mechanical instruments, medicinal herbs, and great elixirs.
The enumeration of passion, the seed-portion, the union of the couple, the excrement, the coloring, the extraction, the oil, the petals, and the transmitters. (Rasārṇava 2.5)

He who knows the enhancement of color, softness, the digestion (jāraṇā) of both the "child" and the "bound" [mercury], as well as the sky-walking (khecarī) and earth-walking (bhūcarī) [states], is considered a Guru. (Rasārṇava 2.6)
One who understands place, time, and ritual action; who is endowed with compassion and courtesy;
who is free from greed and deceit; and who is devoted to the practice of mantra—(Ras 2.7).
Endowed with the marks of a maritime [sailor], profound, and affectionate toward his guru;
always delighting in the worship of the deities, the fire, the circle of yoginīs, and the family (kula);
the disciple should be disciplined, knowledgeable in the tantras, truthful, and firm in his vows. (Ras_2.8)
O Goddess, those men whose hands are marked with signs such as a water-jar, a spade, a banner, or a conch shell should be employed for the accomplishment of treasure-finding. (Rasārṇava 2.9)
Powerful great beings with black and red eyes, crooked noses, and who are always cruel, are praised for the accomplishment of subterranean dwellings. (Ras 2.10)
One should employ those who have fleshless heads, red hair, and are free from sloth;
who are firm and have warm feet, for the practice of alchemy. (Rasāyana 2.11)
O Goddess, at the outset one should examine the practitioners who are well-composed, namely Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, in their proper order. (Rasārṇava 2.12)
O Dear One, those practitioners who have conquered their senses, endure hardships, are endowed with constant diligence, and are both heroic and learned, are highly praised. (Rasārṇava 2.13)

Those who are devoid of the initiation into mercury (rasadīkṣā), who lack the aforementioned characteristics, who are subverters [of the tradition], and who are devoted to sin—one should avoid them with great effort. (Rasārṇava 2.14)

One should avoid that woman who is of evil conduct, of wicked behavior, cruel, fond of quarreling, gluttonous, ill-intentioned, owl-eyed, merciless, and one who speaks in disparagement of the *rasas*. (Ras 2.15)
O lady of excellent hips, even if the entire circle of the earth were filled with such women as these, there would be no woman equal to one who is a binder of passion (rasabandhakī). (Ras 2.16)
A woman who is menstruating during the dark fortnight is known as a *kākiṇī*; likewise, a woman who wears a saffron-colored garment is called a *kāñcikācinī*. (Ras 2.17)
A woman who is menstruating on both sides [of her body] is considered a Kīkaṇī. Ras_2.18 //
In the bright fortnight, that woman who has reached her season should wear a yellow garment.
A woman endowed with fresh youth, beautiful in form, possessing a charming smile, having fine hair, and who always delights in a diet of milk; Ras_2.20.
She who always speaks kindly, who delights in the discourse of the Śiva scriptures, whose face is shaped like a lotus, and whose gaze has the form of a blue water-lily. (Ras 2.21)
Her teeth are like diamonds, her lower lip is like coral;
O Goddess, her two breasts are both high, full, and symmetrical. (Ras 2.22)
She whose vulva resembles the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree and whose labia are even, and whose feet are fleshy, smooth, rounded, and covered with whorled hair; (2.23)
Dark-complexioned, slender-waisted, and thin, devoted to Śiva, she is to be known as a *padminī*—serene and with eyes like those of a deer. (Ras 2.24)
On the full moon or the new moon day, it is menstruating once every fortnight;
this substance known as *kākiṇī*, which bestows mercury, has six varieties as previously described. (Rasārṇava 2.25)
For him with whom Mahādeva is pleased, alchemy (rasāyana) is perfected;
by that very [grace], O Goddess of the gods, one should perform the works of mercury. (Rasārṇava 2.26)
For his intellect, being stainless, is certain in the accomplishment of the elixir;
therefore, both the teacher and the disciple previously mentioned shall partake in success. (Rasāyana 2.27)
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, from where does a practitioner obtain a woman with such characteristics, since here [in this world] there is no characteristic that corresponds to the [ideal] form? (Ras 2.28)
Wherever a characteristic exists, there meditation does not exist;
or else, by whom could form be produced for that which is devoid of form? (Ras_2.29)
O Maheśvara, where have you seen these three characteristics? O Lord, tell me that means by which this [state] is produced. (Ras 2.30)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret which is difficult even for the gods to obtain—the birth from my father Sadāśiva and that which occurred within the womb of Caṇḍikā. (Ras 2.31)
O Goddess, their intellect shall become stainless in the accomplishment of the elixir;
free from pride, they should cause the Tvaritā mantra to be given and should recite it. (Rasārṇava 2.32)
She who recites the *lakṣa* mantra becomes *sulakṣaṇā*;
having bound the *khecarī* mudrā, she should recite the *pheṭkārabhairavī*. Ras_2.33 //
"This Caṇḍikā is my mother, and my birth was from the Destroyer of Tripura;
I am born as Kālikā"—thus she should remember herself. (Ras 2.34)
She may declare the past, the present, and the future within the three worlds;
her companions are such as their own destiny shall make them.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, vessel of all knowledge, I ask about the initiation into the Rasa [of mercury] for the benefit of practitioners indeed. (Ras 2.36)
The illustrious Bhairava said: Listen, O Bhairavī, to this unprecedented state which I describe to you;
listen therefore to the exposition of the ritual for initiation into the Rasa. 2.37.
Where the king is devoted to policy, powerful, and intent on righteousness, and where the minister knows the true essence of dharma and is endowed with devotion and faith; // Ras_2.38 //
In this regard, one should perform the rite of mercury-binding (rasabandha) and the elixir (rasāyana) in any place where people devoted to Maheśvara reside. (Rasārṇava 2.39)
One should cause [the ritual] to be performed in a secluded place where no animals are found, in a well-guarded, level spot, free from all disturbances. (Ras 2.40)
In a secluded, pure, and delightful place, provided with walls and moats, protected by doors and bolts, and filled with various flowering trees. (Ras 2.41)
Abounding with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, graced by ruddy geese, endowed with clusters of divine medicinal herbs, and possessing dark-green grassy banks with water; (Ras 2.42)

O Supreme Goddess, one should cause [the temple] to be constructed in a palace garden adorned with groves of white water-lilies, blue lotuses, white lotuses, and plantain trees, and variegated with paintings. (Ras 2.43)
In its center, O Goddess of the gods, is a structure joined with intoxicated elephants, provided with windows, and emitting smoke that rises upward. (Rasārṇava 2.44)
It was adorned with red banners, equipped with all necessary implements, and provided with various medicines, husks, wood, forest lotuses, and dwellings. (Ras 2.45)
In which the deities of the directions are painted, Vināyaka is duly worshipped, and it is established by Umā and Īśa and protected by the world-protectors. (Ras 2.46)
One should construct a pavilion with either one or two stories;
then, O Goddess, during the bright fortnight, when the moon and the stars are in a favorable position, one should proceed. (Rasārṇava 2.47)

On an auspicious lunar day and at a favorable moment, under a rising sign aspected by gentle planets, he, having bathed and wearing white garments, white garlands, and white unguents, [should proceed]. (Ras 2.48)
Having worshipped the young girls with honey, clarified butter, curd, milk, and sesame seeds, [on a site] smeared with the dung of a tawny cow and surrounded by golden jars; (Ras 2.49)
O Goddess of the Gods, upon that hand-stand constructed there with bricks, strewn with barley and white mustard seeds, and adorned with perfumes and garlands; (Ras 2.50)

O beloved, having carved a stone slab and secured it with a stone bolt, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) using the *rasāṅkuśa* mantra upon the fingers, the heart, and other parts of the body. (Rasārṇava 2.51)
O Dear One, one should place a mercury-liṅga there together with gold;
"Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ" is declared to be the root mantra of the king of elixirs (sūtarāja). (Rasāyana 2.52)

O Dear One, one should invoke the goddess Rasāṅkuśī with the root mantra within that [maṇḍala], after having worshipped the guardians of the directions outside the square in their proper order. (Rasārṇava 2.53)
And Nandin, Mahākāla, the mighty Bhṛṅgirīṭa, Kumbhakarṇa, Sugrīva, Bhṛṅgīka, and Dṛḍhāyudha. (Ras 2.54)
Having arranged [the deities] fourfold at the door, one should worship them on the right and left;
having worshipped Śukra in the east, one should worship Skanda in the domain of Agni (the southeast).

Then one should place Rudra in the south, Pavana in the southwest (nairṛta), Śiva in the western part, and Pāvaka in the northwest (vāyu). One should place Umā in the northern part, and the Pervasive One (Vyāpaka) in the northeast (īśa).
Lepikā, Kṣepikā, Kṣārikā, Rañjikā, Lohaṭī, Bandhakārī, Bhūcarī, and Mṛtyunāśinī. (Rasārṇava 2.57)
Vibhūti and Khecarī— these ten Dūtīs are to be worshipped in sequence upon the petals of an eight-petaled lotus, including the upper and lower petals.
Mākṣika, vimala, śaila, capala, rasaka, sasyaka, and gandhatāla are [the minerals] according to the sequence starting from the east. (Rasāyana 2.59)
The Rudras have eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes;
their crowns are adorned with the crescent moon, they have blue throats, and the bull is their emblem. (Ras 2.60)
O Maheśānī, all the eight Vidyeśvaras, each bearing his own respective color,
are likewise to be worshipped in the second eight-petalled lotus.
In the pericarp, however, starting from the east, there is first the quartet of Śaktis:
Mālinī, Hemaśakti, Parāśakti, and Balā; Aparā, Vajraśakti, and Kānti are known as the supreme and the intermediate. (Ras_2.62)
And in the midst of those powers is the omniscient Rasabhairava, resembling pure crystal, five-faced, and three-eyed. (Rasārṇava 2.63)
With blazing, fierce, reddish-brown eyes, a face with a flaming tongue,
flaming eyebrows, and flaming hair, he was difficult to behold and seated upon a corpse.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, wearing a tiger skin, having a serpent as his sacred thread, and possessing a bull as his emblem. (Ras 2.65)
One should worship the eighteen-armed deity, whose face is slightly smiling,
as the complete Śiva by means of the mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables.
And learn from me the mantra of the Lord of Tastes (Raseśvara) as it is being told. (Rasārṇava 2.67)
Oṃ hrīṃ krīṃ! To the Lord of Taste, Mahākāla, the one of great power, Aghorabhairava, Vajravīra, Krodhakaṅkāla, kṣlauḥ kṣlaḥ! Ras_2.68 //
In his lap [he saw] the Great Goddess, adorned with jewel ornaments,
radiant as refined gold, clad in yellow garments, and possessing three eyes.
She is graced by a pearl parasol between two white chowries, and she holds a goad and a rosary in her two right hands. (Ras 2.70)
With her two left hands she displays the noose and the gesture of fearlessness; she has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament;
she is the Great Goddess Rasāṅkuśī, blue-necked and full of compassion.
O Goddess of the Suras, one should worship with the five-syllable Vidyā for the sake of attaining mastery over mercury:
namely, the Vāgbhava, the Bhuvaneśī, and the Śrībīja. (Rasārṇava 2.72)
The *mādana* and the *śakti-bīja* are the Vidyā, which is extremely difficult to obtain;
[one should worship it] with incense, lamps, food offerings, flowers, betel, and sandalwood. (Rasārṇava 2.73)

Having performed the worship according to the ritual rules with the resonant recitations of the *śāntipāṭha*, with the sounds of hymns and auspicious chants, and accompanied by the ringing of bells, Ras_2.74.
One should diligently offer a bali-oblation with the Aghora mantra to the spirits, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas for the pacification of all obstacles. (Ras 2.75)
O Goddess, this [mantra] joined with the Aghora-mantra, beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, is the performer of all rites and the destroyer of obstacles and calamities. (Ras 2.76)

Having recited the *rasāṅkuśī* mantra itself according to one's capacity, O Goddess of Gods, one should prepare the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) as a vulva-circle (*yonicakra*) provided with a girdle (*mekhalā*). (Ras 2.77)
There, having performed the fire-oblation (homa) in due order with clarified butter and sesame seeds,
one should then place, O Goddess, a water-pot filled with milk and provided with fruit.
Equipped with the five jewels and wrapped in cloths,
one should consecrate it there with each of the eighteen branches of learning individually.

Having worshipped the arghya vessel, which is filled with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and adorned with sprouts, and having sprinkled the practitioner with water from the vardhanī vessel, [one should proceed]. (Ras 2.80)

The knower of mantras, having thus sprinkled [the disciple] one hundred and eight times with the water from the arghya vessel according to the ritual procedure, should then do so with the water from the pitcher.
O Goddess, one should instruct the science and cause the practitioner of mercury (rasasādhaka) to recite it;
likewise, one should appropriately instruct the Kumārīs, Yoginīs, Yogins, and Sādhakas. (Rasārṇava 2.82)
One should satisfy [the deities] with food and drink and hold a vigil there; thus initiated, O Kṣuranāyikā, the practitioner [proceeds]. (Ras_2.83)

There, within the thread of the self consisting of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should contemplate the Vidyā composed of the five great elements, endowed with the five colors, and having the nature of the five seed-syllables. (Rasāyana 2.84)
O Dear One, having bound the mudrā of Rasāṅkuśī, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
O Goddess of Gods, for such a person, Rasabhairava is accomplished without obstacle. (Ras 2.85)
The supreme recitation (japa) consists of [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, performed at the conclusion of the libation (tarpaṇa).
Non-violence is the sandalwood paste, truth is the flower, and non-stealing is the incense. (Ras 2.86)
O Maheśānī, celibacy is the great lamp, the bell that wards off grasping;
it is milk-rice, whose very essence is compassion for all beings.
Keeping this secret, one should worship the Goddess; he shall become a vessel for spiritual accomplishments.
He should recite this [mantra] a thousand or even a hundred times at the three junctions of the day.

By the grace of her command, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the mercury that moves through the sky (khecarī-rasa) is born, and the divine medicinal herbs are likewise perfected for him. (Rasārṇava 2.89)
Just as one who has mounted a rutting elephant in the forest without a goad perishes,
so too does one who knows the goad of the *rasas* perish upon attaining the sovereign *rasa*.
One who desires success in every respect must contemplate the entire range of mercury applications together with the knowledge of a guru who belongs to a true lineage. (Rasārṇava 2.91)
Now, for the introduction of the questions, one should meditate with a concentrated mind upon the previously mentioned Rasabhairava; one should practice until absorbed in that. (Ras 2.92)
Having fixed the mind upon the stainless *anāhata* at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
and having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) followed immediately by the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), one should,
with a concentrated mind, recite the mantra of the Lord of Mercury (*rasendra*) according to one's capacity. (Rasārṇava 2.93)
Having again made a square, one should draw a six-cornered maṇḍala in the center, measuring one cubit or two cubits, using pure rice grains. (Rasāyana 2.94)
In a place smeared with fragrances, one should worship with sandalwood and other such substances.
O Goddess, one should place the previously mentioned Rasabhairava in the pericarp;
one should then assign the group of six deities, beginning with Mahākāla, to the hexagon. (Ras 2.96)
One should place Mahākāla, Mahābala, Aghora, Vajravīraka, Krodha, and Kaṅkāla, and worship them with the garland mantras. (Ras_2.97)

Oṃ hrīṃ krauṃ kṣlaiṃ kṣlaṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrūḥ huṃ phaṭ! To the Lord of Mercury (Raseśvara), to Mahākālabhairava, to him of fierce form, to him whose eyes are black and tawny: descend, descend; cause to descend, cause to descend; speak, speak; cause to speak, cause to speak; declare the auspicious and the inauspicious, declare them; perform great protection, perform it; grant the accomplishment of mercury! Thus are the garland-mantras (mālāmantra).
Oṃ, homage to the heart of Mahākālabhairava; Oṃ, svāhā to the head of Mahābalabhairava;
Oṃ, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock of Aghorabhairava.
Oṃ, to Vajravīrabhairava, for the armor, hūṃ! Oṃ, to Krodhabhairava, for the eyes, vauṣaṭ!
Oṃ, to Kaṅkālabhairava, for the weapon, phaṭ!
In all cases, [the mantra] ends with "svāhā. Thus are the placements on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). Likewise, one should first perform the placements on the fingers (*aṅgulīnyāsa*).
These are the root mantras for the six-limbed worship.
Thus, one should worship with the letters of the ritual placement (nyāsa) using incense and flowers.
One should place a full water-pot in the center and a shallow bowl (śarāva) together with rice.
Upon that, one should place a ghee lamp and consecrate the wick with mantras.
Having brought a young girl or a very handsome youth—
one, two, three, four, or five, according to what is available—
he should worship them with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings. (Ras 2.100)
One should assign the mantra to each individual part, as well as the deities beginning with the Heart.
Then, having gazed upon that lamp, all those maidens there,
as well as the deities and the youths, perceive the auspicious or inauspicious [signs] within the lamp;
the maidens then declare whether there will be success or failure.
Having understood the introduction to the questions, one should proceed with the work of alchemy. 2.103.

O Goddess of the lords of gods, he who has previously purified his self through the lord of mercury (rasendra) shall not abandon the cultivation of mercury even if he dies and is born again for seven lifetimes. (Rasārṇava 2.104)
Having thus understood what is auspicious and inauspicious, and being endowed with the grace of the deity,
one should worship the goddess Rasāṅkuśī in the pavilion as before.
Having also worshipped the preceptor with incense, garlands, sandalwood, and other offerings,
and having presented the bali-oblation with the Aghora mantra, one should then perform the ritual action.
The medicinal herbs are in the pavilion in the east; extraction by liquid and sweating are in the south-east;
the smelting of metals is in the south; and grinding and so forth are in the south-west. (Rasārṇava 2.107)
O Dear One, liquefaction occurs in the western direction, blowing in the northwestern;
the excellence of color in the northern, and the transmutation of the essence in the northeastern. (Rasārṇava 2.108)
O leader of the gods, having placed the seat of the Guru in the center,
O lady of excellent countenance, the practitioner must perform the rites beginning with *niyāmana* and ending with *krāmaṇa* using the mantra *rasāṅkuśa*. (Rasāyana 2.109)
O Goddess of the lords of gods, that Rasabhairava who was described previously—his knee is Sadyojāta and his secret part is Vāmadeva. (Ras 2.110)
His heart is Aghora, his face is known as Tatpuruṣa;
Īśāna extends as far as the middle of the eyebrows, and the half-moon is on the forehead. (Ras 2.111)
O Goddess of the gods, there is the Bindu; above that Bindu stands the Nada.
Between the forehead and the head, Śakti is situated right there. (Rasāyana 2.112)
Pervasive, it resides at the aperture of Brahmā; above that, however, is Unmanā.
Unmanā is the state of Unmanī, the imperishable station of Unmanā. (Ras 2.113)
Above that is the supreme reality, abiding in the void, higher than the highest;
it is the void, the void, and again the void—the triple-void, free from all affliction.
The sky, the firmament, the void, the ether, and the absolute space—partless, stainless, eternal, waveless, and free from affliction. (Ras 2.115)

One should always meditate upon Rasabhairava within one's own body as being of such a nature: free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), without support (*nirādhāra*), devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), yet the sphere of all qualities (*guṇagocara*). (Ras 2.116)
And when one meditates immovably, and when the mind is likewise immovable, then the mercury is bound within the midst of fire, becoming as motionless as well. (Rasārṇava 2.117)
And when the meditative absorption wavers, the essence does not remain in the fire. (Rasāyana 2.118)
Outside the mandala at night, one should worship the yakṣas, gandharvas, piśācas, and likewise the rākṣasas with liquor, fish, meat, and other offerings. (Ras 2.119)
Obstacles to the performance of rituals and obstacles to the fruits thereof arise by the millions;
therefore, for the pacification of each of those, one should first perform worship and practice the sixfold grace of Vaṭukeśvara. (Rasārṇava 2.120)

Furthermore, at the conclusion of the ritual, having honored the child with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭāṣṭaka*), one should employ that perfected substance which bestows accomplishment. (Rasārṇava 2.121)
Once success is achieved, one should abandon the debate and leave that place;
when the great elixir is well-accomplished, one should wander for alms like a honey-gatherer. (Rasāyana 2.122)

If an obstacle arises due to negligence once the binding of the mercury has been performed, the pacification of the mercury must be carried out; one should not cause agitation of the mercury. (Rasāyana 2.123)

O Goddess, one should not show the elixir; one should not let it fall into the hand of a woman. One should not speak of the secret to a woman, for one must indeed conceal the substance from them. (Rasāyana 2.124)
One should not act with the wealth of others, one should not touch the wives of others, one should never eat the food of others, and one should not place trust in others. (Ras 2.125)
It should not be given to those of wicked intellect who come as beggars under the guise of a social gathering.
On the eighth day, on the full moon, on the new moon, on the beginnings of the yugas,
during the solstices and the equinoxes, and especially on the fourteenth day,
one should perform the Festival of Essence (rasotsava) according to one's means. (Ras 2.127)
O Goddess, for one who performs such a festival of rasa endowed with devotion, various sins, including the killing of a Brahmin, are destroyed. (Ras 2.128)
By this method, wherever practitioners perform worship, neither disease nor misfortune prevails there, nor do epidemics exert their power. (Rasāyana 2.129)

Having thus established this kind of worship in the mercury according to the prescribed rule, the subsequent ritual (paścātkarma) must be performed by those desiring their own welfare. (Rasāyana 2.130)
But for one who performs it otherwise, success does not arise;
rather, misfortune, the apprehension of sin, and the ruin of the intellect indeed occur. (Ras 2.131)

O beloved, those born of noble family destroy even the wisdom that has arisen through contempt, the onset of disease, doubt at every step, laziness, excessive greed, and by speaking ill of others (Ras 2.132).

"O Goddess of the Gods, tell me how one who has been initiated and knows the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) should perform the operations of mercury (rasakarma); what else do you wish to hear? (Rasārṇava 2.133)
The Third Chapter [The Depositions of Mantras]. The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, Protector of the World, Master of the Universe!
Explain the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), which is beneficial for the practice of alchemy (rasakarma).
The illustrious Bhairava said: O Goddess, I shall now further proclaim another [form], the Mantra-body Rasāṅkuśī;
this is the fifth house, difficult even for gods and dānavas to attain.
There are four principal houses, and the house of Haṃsa is the fifth;
therein, in the fifth house, resides the accomplishment beginning with the letter *ma*.
Just as form has the linga as its support, Māyā is the possessor of the linga (liṅginī);
she is to be known by means of the sky, while the line of the Bhaga is in the fifth [element]. (Ras_3.4)
Having first uttered the *praṇava*, then the unsurpassed seed-syllable of sound,
followed by the syllable *hrīṃ* and the syllable *krīṃ*, and immediately thereafter the mind of the *haṃsa*.
The lord of practitioners should take up the great mantra of Kālapāśa;
for a great undertaking, however, he should employ that mantra as a gatekeeper and [the mantra of] Rasāṅkuśī.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; for him, the great siddhi proceeds.
Then, one should have [the disciple] swallow the feces of a young child using the same [substance]. (Ras 3.7)
O Supreme Goddess, one should have the ashes from that very funeral pyre collected;
that place is an excellent field, and there the lord of mercury (rasendra) resides. (Rasārṇava 3.8)
One should cleanse the place with the *mārjanī*; the one called *kubjikā* is indeed the *khecarī*.
O Goddess, she consists of thirty-two syllables and is established within the five *nādas*. (Ras 3.9)
Then, four perfected ones (siddhas) and eighteen persons are traditionally taught;
joined with the five objects, there is furthermore the fivefold meditation.
It is joined with the six Yoginīs, endowed with the sequence of twenty-seven, possessed of eighty-one words, and associated with five enclosures. (Ras 3.11)
By this sequential method, one should worship the broom;
by this, one should sweep the field where the lord of mercury resides. (Rasāyana 3.12)
One should have Caṇḍaghaṇṭā fashioned right there on the plastering;
that goddess Caṇḍaghaṇṭā is established in the eastern house. (Ras 3.13)
The goddess Caṇḍabhairavikā resides in the southern house;
with that [substance], O fair-faced one, one should take cow dung for the purpose of smearing. (Ras 3.14)
The goddess Caṇḍakāpālinī is established in the northern house;
taking water, one should smear the mandala ground with it. (Ras 3.15)
One should place the seventeen-syllable Kālī-mantra upon the grinding stone (khalapāṣāṇa), and one should employ the thirty-two-syllable Ghoramantra upon the mortar (mardaka). (Rasārṇava 3.16)
O Goddess, one who is consecrated by the mantra of Kālapāśa should take up the sour gruel;
thus does the Khecarī family effect a union with virtuous action. (Rasārṇava 3.17)
The eighty-eight thousand divine sky-farers who reside there—all of them become his servants and grind the medicinal herbs for him. (Rasāyana 3.18)
For all of them, however, there is a single mantra joined with four syllables:
"So 'haṃ haṃsaḥ.
This is the *vidyā* of the *khecarīs*, known by the name *Kulakhecarī*. (Ras 3.19)
Having placed mustard seeds and rock salt there, that *vidyā* is the *Kulakhecarī*;
one should consecrate the *kāñjika* (sour gruel) therein with the *mantrarāja*, the *Rasāṅkuśī*. (Ras 3.20)
There, one should mutter the *astravidyā* known previously by Bhārgava;
O Dear One, having crushed a brick with molasses, [one should take] that crushed juice. (Rasārṇava 3.21)
What need is there to speak of the King of Mantras? Nor is the word of Triśiras required;
one should apply that six-limbed [practice] and then hold it with haste. (Ras 3.22)
One should apply the great mantra named Ḍāmara to the vessels;
one should apply the great vidyā Cintāmaṇi to the armor. (Ras 3.23)
One should employ that great mantra of Caṇḍikā in a vessel;
O lady of excellent limbs, one should place the ninefold vidyā upon husks and cow dung. (Rasārṇava 3.24)
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, one should place the goddess Tripurābhairavī in black mustard and sour gruel; Kālarātri, however, should be placed in molasses. (Rasārṇava 3.25)
O Goddess, one should place the three-eyed, three-peaked [deity] of fire;
and in the water, one should place the eighty-four Caṇḍikās.
O Dear One, the Kṣetrapāla and Aghorāstra mantras should be deposited in the crucible chamber;
one should likewise employ the Mahāpāśupatāstra in the crucible. (Rasārṇava 3.27)
O Goddess, one should employ this collection of mantras in the place of the mercury;
then, O Beloved, the fruit is accomplished for that practitioner. (Rasāyana 3.28)
One should recite the great mantra Rasāṅkuśa within the heart;
one should cause all other Yoginī mantras and all women to recite it as well. (Ras 3.29)

One should keep the King of Mantras, Rasāṅkuśa, secret by that very means; likewise, one should guard the Praṇava from women, for it is like the heart of women—a great violation of the samaya. (Ras 3.30)
O my beloved, those mantras beginning with Kubjikā which have been revealed by me have indeed agitated the three worlds, yet they do not acknowledge me. (Ras 3.31)
Through the knowledge of the goad of flavor, the three worlds shall come under one's control. (Rasāṅkuśa 3.32)
Having understood this placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), the practitioner who knows the proportions of the crucible fire and performs the operations of mercury attains perfection. (Rasārṇava 3.33)
The Fourth Chapter: [Description of the Yantra, Crucible, and Fire].
The Goddess said:
Without knowing the dimensions of the yantra, the crucible, and the fire, even one who knows the mantras [cannot succeed].
O Great God, what do they do? You should tell that to me.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Mercury, the secondary minerals (uparasa), and metals; cloth, sour gruel (kāñjika), and viḍa salt;
bellows, metal vessels, and the grinding stone with its mortar for crushing. (Rasārṇava 4.2)
A furnace, a curved tube, cow dung, heartwood for fuel, clay vessels, and mortars and pestles; (Rasāyana 4.3).
A pair of tongs, a cloth-strip tongs, an earthen vessel, and an iron ladle;
weights and balances, cutting tools, and a touchstone. (Rasāyana 4.4)
Bamboo tubes, metal tubes, saline earth, charcoal, as well as medicinal herbs, oils, acids, salts, alkalis, poisons, and secondary poisons. (Rasakalpa 4.5)
Having thus gathered the accumulations, one should practice the application of the rite.

When the interior of a vessel is filled halfway with a liquid substance and its mouth is tilted, and mercury suspended by a thread is placed within that vessel so that it rests upon the bottom, one should subject it to heat; this is known as the *dolāyantra* (swing apparatus). (Rasakalpa 4.7)
Having prepared two iron crucibles measuring twelve finger-breadths in size, one should place a slightly perforated crucible there, filled with sulfur. (Rasārṇava 4.8)
One should place that [substance] into another crucible containing mercury;
there shall be water beneath the mercury, while fire is applied from above and below to kindle it. (Rasāyana 4.9)
O blessed lady, one should carefully cause onion juice, strained through cloth, to be administered in abundance after having thoroughly saturated the mercury and sulphur with it. (Rasārṇava 4.10)
Having placed [the substance] in a vessel, place another firm vessel over it; one should carefully seal the joint with clay and indeed with cloth. (Rasāyanasamhitā 4.11)
One should always apply a *kapota*-type seal (*puṭa*) inside another vessel using a fire of one *karṣa* weight;
below the apparatus, one should provide either a fire of dried cow-dung (*karīṣāgni*) or a fierce fire (*tīvrāgni*). (Rasakaumudī 4.12)
One should proceed in this manner for three days, and thereafter release the apparatus;
one should not perform the operation in cold water or on a cold hearth, but rather in hot water or on a heated hearth. (Rasārṇava 4.13)
In that process, the mercury is neither consumed nor does it go anywhere;
by this sequential method, one should perform the digestion of sulphur. (Rasakalpa 4.14)
Fire above, water below, and the collection of mercury in the middle—this is the crucible apparatus (*mūṣāyantra*), O Goddess; it causes the digestion of mica and other substances. (Rasārṇava 4.15)
I shall now describe the *garbhayantra*, which is the means for producing the ash of *piṣṭikā*:
one should take a firm crucible made of clay, four finger-breadths in length. (Rasārṇava 4.16)
One should make the mouth circular with a middle width of three finger-breadths;
there should be twenty parts of iron and one part of guggulu. (Rasārṇava 4.17)
Having ground it very finely, one should add water repeatedly;
then one should apply a coating to the crucible and place the paste at its base. (Rasāyana 4.18)

One should apply gentle heat to the mercury on the ground using a fire fueled by husks and grain-chaff for one day and night or for three nights; thus the mercury will attain the state of ash. (Rasārṇava 4.19)

In the processes of digestion (jāraṇa), killing (māraṇa), and the coloring (rañjana) of the king of mercury, there is one supreme machine which is the vital point, wherein medicinal herbs possess great power. (Rasārṇava 4.20)
And this mercury, when devoid of medicinal herbs, is bound by means of a mechanical device through force;
it moves everywhere, except for that which possesses the characteristics of a mountain (a crucible). (Rasārṇava 4.21)
For even a clod of earth, when drawn by the deities, goes along;
therefore, a wise person should not disregard the power of the machine alone. (Ras 4.22)
Indeed, through the conjunction of mantra and medicinal herbs, this [practitioner] brings about perfect accomplishment.
Here, the non-terrible (aghora) mantra is to be recited; at the conclusion of the recitation, one should worship the mercury. (Rasāyana 4.23)
The ritual must be performed in solitude; otherwise, it will be seen by others and become fruitless.

There is no exhaustion of the mercury (gandhaka), nor shall there be any exhaustion of the juice (rasa); rather, the exhaustion of the apparatus (yantra) is to be recognized when the operation within the apparatus undergoes transformation. In the absence of magnetite (kāntaloha), one should have the apparatus made of iron. (Rasāyana 4.25)
Without knowing the signs of the fire, there will be a loss of half the mercury;
for one who knows the method for the exhaustion of the apparatus, there will be a loss of only a fourth part. (Rasāyana 4.26)
In two months, it attains the second part, and in three months, the third part; for wherever this [mercury] is processed and remains, it indeed endures the great fire. (Rasāyanatantra 4.27)
Having filled one earthen bowl with sand, one should place another bowl upon it;
there, one should cook it slowly over a mild fire. (Rasāyana 4.28)
Then, with the five alkalis, urines, and salts, *viḍa* is subsequently processed;
this is known as *haṃsapāka* by those skilled in the meaning of the *yantra* and *tantra*. (Rasakaumudī 4.29)
The clay may be black, red, yellow, or white in color;
the first is considered the best, the last the lowest, and those in between are regarded as middling. (Rasāyana 4.30)
O beautiful goddess, for the procedure of the crucible (*koṣṭhikā*), earth mixed with burnt grain husks, or even that fashioned from a curved tube, is recommended. (Rasārṇava 4.31)
The kiln is burnt, the husks are burnt, and the clay of the anthill is burnt; the dung of goats and horses is burnt until it has reached a state of blackness. (Ras 4.32)
One should grind the leaves of the *vāsaka* plant together with the clay of an anthill using water heated by fire, until it reaches a state of smoothness. (Rasakalpa 4.33)
One should crush it with that [substance] and bind the crooked tube and the crucible. (Rasārṇava 4.34)
The charcoal is burnt, the husks are burnt, and the clay from the anthill is burnt;
the rags, the charcoal, and the dross cannot be pierced even by a thunderbolt. (Rasāyana 4.35)
Six parts of burnt charcoal and one part of black earth, along with rags, charcoal, and dross—this is proclaimed as the *vajramūṣā* crucible. (Rasakalpa 4.36)
Chaff, cloth, burnt earth, and four parts of clay combined with *kupī* stone are proclaimed as the excellent crucible (*varamūṣā*). (Rasāyana 4.37)
The crucible is known to be of two kinds: the *prakāśa* (open) and the *andhamūṣā* (closed). 4.38.
O Goddess of the gods, the *prakāśamūṣā* is shaped like a shallow bowl;
it is highly praised by experts for the sublimation of substances. (Rasāyana 4.39)
The blind crucible (andhamūṣā) should be made resembling the shape of a cow’s udder, provided with a lid, and having its mouth slightly raised. (Rasārṇava 4.40)
Likewise, in leaf-paste, in coloring, and in the blending of duals, that same [pitch] which is slightly defective, slow, and deep is suitable for *sāraṇā*. (Ras 4.41)
Sesame ash in two parts combined with one part of brick is to be known as the "ash crucible" (bhasmamūṣā), which is beneficial for the purification of silver. (Rasaka 4.42)
O lady of excellent complexion, for the purification of silver, two parts of alkali from cow-dung and one part of brick, along with portions of clay, are the best [ingredients]. (Rasāyana 4.43)

Mixed with the group of red substances, saturated with the group of red substances, and having an ointment made from the group of red substances applied, it is excellent for all purifications. (Rasāyana 4.44)
Mixed with white substances, saturated with white substances, and having an ointment made from white substances, it is excellent for purifications involving white [substances]. (Rasāyana 4.45)
Mixed with the group of fecal matter (viḍavarga), it seeks stability during digestion;
one should effect its thorough carrying through (nirvāhaṇa) by means of that which is smeared with the group of blood-ingredients (raktavarga). (Rasārṇava 4.46)
One should apply a coating to the crucible with viṣa, ṭaṅkaṇa, and guñjā;
this should be done in the open air, or alternatively, by applying charcoal. (Rasārṇava 4.47)
Having placed the substance in that crucible, the wise one should cause it to revolve;
O Goddess, the coating is a color-sealing (*varṇapuṭa*) made from red clay, sea salt, earth, and mercury. (Rasāyana 4.48)
O Goddess of the Gods, when gold is being processed, its luster is yellow; in silver, it is white;
in copper, it resembles blue; and in iron, it is black in color. (Rasāyana 4.49)
O Goddess, in tin it is flame-colored like a pigeon; in lead, it is dark smoke-colored;
in stone, it is greyish; and in iron, it has a tawny luster. (Rasārṇava 4.50)
In the magnet, it is smoke-colored; in the loadstone, it becomes red;
in the diamond, there are various kinds of flames; and in the *khasattva*, it has a pale white luster. (Rasāyana 4.51)
When there is no spark, nor bubbles, nor a mass of streaks, nor sound, and it has become stable like a gem within the crucible, then they declare the metal to be purified. (Rasāyana 4.52)
The *pratīvāpa* (additive) is to be added first, and immediately after that, the *niṣeka* (infusion).
They know the *chādana* (covering) to be the *pratīvāpa*, and the *majjana* (immersion) to be the *niṣeka*;
they desire the *abhiṣeka* (consecration) to be that which is performed as the *snapana* (bath). (Rasakalpalatā 4.53)
Sowing, impregnation, and bathing—once the [mercury] has been liquefied and attained purity, they desire it to be cooled by heat alone; indeed, it does not desire anything else. (Rasāyana 4.54)
When Vaiśvānara becomes white-radiant and accompanied by sound, it should be known as lohāvarta; then pure sattva falls. (Rasakaumudī 4.55)

O lady of excellent complexion, for the purpose of depositing the elements and the essence of beings, there should be an auspicious small chamber sixteen finger-breadths wide and one cubit long. (Rasāyana 4.56)
One should blow upon the crucible with air until it is completely filled with firm charcoal made from bamboo, khadira, madhūka, or badarī wood;
and one should kindle the fire by means of the nozzle of a bellows. (Rasāyana 4.57)

The chamber should have a wide opening at the top and a contracted interior space, with a long internal lattice-work constructed upon its floor; it should be equal in measure to the throat of a crane.
A curved tube should be provided, and there should be a hollow lotus-shaped nozzle made of clay, which is elongated and cylindrical. (Rasakalpa 4.58)
In a vessel made of clay, or of metal, or even of magnetite;
or in stone, or crystal, or even in one made of pearl-stone. (Rasāyana 4.59)
A very firm mardaka (grinding tool) should be made, four finger-breadths in height;
it should be made of iron, stone, or even of magnetite. (Rasāyana 4.60)
One should effect purification by means of the mantra known as Aghorāstra or the Mahāpāśupata; one should purify the ground with that very same [mantra]. (Ras_4.61)
One should ignite all kinds of fuel and especially solid substances; with that [fire], one should indeed purify the crucible. (Rasāyana 4.62)
One should purify the mercury with that [substance] and place it on an auspicious day;
having placed it upon a mortar, one should meditate upon the form of Śiva. (Rasāyana 4.63)

O Goddess, having obtained the grace of the deity, one who knows the measure of the fire in the crucible of the yantra should also know the medicinal herbs for the sake of attaining perfection in mercury.
The measures for the crucible, the furnace, and the fire have been described, O Goddess of the Gods;
tell me that, O Queen of the Devas, and what else do you wish to hear? (Rasārṇava 4.65)
The Fifth Chapter: [The Determination of Herbs].
The Goddess said:
O Lord of the Gods, [you have explained] the ritual beginning with the binding [of the disciple] and ending with the transference [of power].
You should explain the medicinal plant by which these [qualities] are indeed produced.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Sarpākṣa, Vahni, Karkoṭī, Kañcukī, Jalabindujā, Śatāvarī, Bhṛṅgarāja, Śarapuṅkhā, and Punarnavā. (Rasārṇava 5.2)
Maṇḍūkaparṇī, Matsyākṣī, Brahmadaṇḍī, Śikhaṇḍinī, Anantā, Kākajaṅghā, Kākamācī, and Kapotikā. (Rasakalpa 5.3)
Viṣṇukrāntā, sahacarā, sahādevī, mahābalā, balā, nāgabalā, kṛṣṇā, cakramarda, and kuruṅgiṇī. (Rasakalpa 5.4)
Pāṭhā, āmalakī, nīlī, jvālinī, padmacāriṇī, phaṇi, trijihvā, gojihvā, kokilākṣa, and ghanadhvani. (Rasāyana 5.5)
Ākhuparṇī, triparṇī, dviparṇī, ekaparṇikā, tittiḍī, kṣīriṇī, rāsnā, meṣaśṛṅgī, and kukkuṭī. (Rasakalpa 5.6)
Kṛṣṇaparṇī, Tulasī, Śvetā, and Girikarṇikā—
these are the regulating medicinal herbs, provided with flowers, roots, and leaves;
O lady of excellent vows, a fomentation bath (dolāsveda) should be performed using these roots.
Caṇḍālī, Rākṣasī, Vyāghrī, Khaḍgārī, Gajakarṇikā, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Agnidhamanī, Lāṅgalī, and Bālamocakā. (Rasāyana 5.8)
Red snuhī, red śṛṅgī, raktikā, blue citraka, śṛgālajihvā, bṛhatī, vajrā, cakrī, and rājikā. (Rasakalpa 5.9)
Ekavīrā, Narakasā, Rudantī, Brahmacāriṇī, Uccaṭā, Māninīkanda, Kumārī, and Raktacitraka. (Rasārṇava 5.10)
Lakṣmī, śākhoṭaka, kañcukī, meṣaśṛṅgikā, himāvatī, somalatā, modā, vyāghranakhī, and śamī. (Ras 5.11)
Kāñcanī, Vanarājī, Kākamācī, Keśinī, Ajamārī, Koṭarākṣī, Hanūmatī, and Aṅganāyikā. (Ras 5.12)
Narajīvā, hemapuṣpī, kākamuṇḍī, kālikā, toyavallī, gajārī, haṃsāṅghrī, kuhukaṃvikā, tāmbūlī, sūryabhaktā, and rasanirjīvakārikā; [these are the plants]. (Rasakalpa 5.13)
Bitter gourd (kaṭutumbī), gosandhī, devadālī, indravāruṇī, vākucī, seeds of brahma, cotton, and black cumin (kṛṣṇajīraka). (Rasakalpa 5.14)
Kaṅgunī, kṛṣṇakanaka, śvetārka, pipīlijam, dantinī, yavaciñcā, karkoṭī, and kāravallikā. (Rasāyana 5.15)
Gojihvā, kākajaṅghā, mahākālī, śambarī,
śvetaguñjā, sitāṅkola, paṭolī, and bilva—
one seed of each of these medicinal herbs should be used to kill rasabhairava. (Rasārṇava 5.16)
Red snuhī, somalatā, rudantī, red citraka, śākhoṭakī, dagdharuhā, modinī, and vṛddhadāruka. (Rasārṇava 5.17)
Triśūlī, kṛṣṇamārjārī, cakrikā, kṣīrakukkuṭī, devadālī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, kākamācī, and hanūmatī. (Rasakalpa 5.18)
Nīlajyotis, tṛṇajyotis, utkaṭā, hemavallarī, tridaṇḍī, brahmadaṇḍī, cakrāṅkī, and sthalapadminī. (Rasakalpalatā 5.19)
Nāgajihvā, Nāgakarṇī, Vīrā, Vartulaparṇikā, Arkapattrī, Vaṃśapattrī, Tāmraparṇī, and likewise Īśvarī,
Indurī, and Devadeveśī— these, O Dear One, are the binders of mercury. (Rasārṇava 5.20)
Through substances—whether stationary or mobile—that possess intense fragrance, taste, and touch, the mercury is killed and indeed bound by means of sweating and rubbing. (Rasārṇava 5.21)
Sūryāvarta, kadalī, vandhyā, kośātakī, vajrakanda, udakakaṇā, kākamācī, and śigruka; Ras_5.22.
O Goddess of gods, *devadālī* and *drāvikā* are proclaimed to remove the defects of the metals and of mercury for the sake of the yogins. (Rasārṇava 5.23)
Kākamācī, ghanarava, kāsamarda, kṛtāñjali, varāhakarṇī, saṭirī, haṃsadāvī, and śatāvarī. (Ras 5.24)
Tāmbūlī, nāginī, brahmī, haṃsapādī, and lakṣaṇā;
arjunī, kṣīranālī, kāravello, and arkapattrikā;
vyāghrī, cavī, and kuravaka—these are the krāmikas, O Goddess worshipped by the gods. (Rasakalpa 5.25)
The Brahmadaṇḍa, the Sudaṇḍa, and the third, the Lohadaṇḍa—these are suitable for alchemy (rasāyana), corresponding respectively to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. (Rasāyanasūtra 5.26)

Bhūpāṭalī, kaumārī, siṃhavallī, śūkarī, hemaparṇī, paṭolī, nāgavallī, and bhṛṅgarāja—these eight are declared to be the medicinal roots (mūlikās). Now listen, O beloved, to the five jewels (pañcaratna). (Rasārṇava 5.27)
O Goddess, Mantrasiddhāsana, Kaṅkālakhecarī,
Indirā, Kṣamāpālī, and Niśācarī as the fifth—
this is the "Five Jewels" (Pañcaratna) for the purification and digestion of mercury. (Rasārṇava 5.28)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, each one of these is praised for the binding of mercury;
O lady of excellent vows, one should seize the five gems with the "Mercury-Goad" (rasāṅkuśa), which bestows the siddhi of moving through the sky upon union with Rasabhairava. (Rasārṇava 5.29)
The three alkalis are borax, nitre, and wood-ash; sesame, apāmārga, kadalī, palāśa, śigru, mocikā, radish, ginger, and tamarind are proclaimed as the vegetable alkalis. (Rasārṇava 5.30)
Amlavetasa, jambīra, luṅga, sour chickpeas (amlacaṇaka), nāraṅga, tintiṇīka, and cāṅgerī are the best among the group of sour substances. (Rasakalpa 5.31)
Sea salt, rock salt, cūlikā salt, sauvarcala salt, and kāca salt—these are proclaimed as the five salts. (Rasakalpa 5.32)
Saktuka, kālakūṭa, sitamustā, śṛṅgī, and kṛṣṇaviṣa—these five are indeed the great poisons. (Rasāyana 5.33)
Snuhī, arka, unmattaka, karavīra, and lāṅgalī—these five are indeed the primary minor poisons (upaviṣa), and their oils are truly excellent.
[The oils] produced from kusumbha, kaṅguṇī, naktā, sesame, and mustard seeds, however, [are used for other purposes]. (Rasakalpa 5.34)
The urine of elephants, horses, goats, and women, with cow's urine as the fifth. 5.35.
Pitta is of five kinds, originating from fish, cows, horses, humans, and peacocks. (Rasakalpa 5.36)
Fat is of five kinds, derived from fish, sheep, snake, elephant, and peacock. (Rasāyana 5.37)
The excrement of pigeons, blue jays, vultures, peacocks, and roosters [is used]. (Rasakalpa 5.38)
Mañjiṣṭhā, kuṅkuma, lākṣā, khadira, and likewise asana—this, O Goddess of Gods, is the red group (raktavarga). Now hear about the yellow group (pītavarga):
kusumbha, kiṃśuka, rātrī, pataṅga, and madayantikā. (Rasakaumudī 5.39)
The white group consists of conch, tortoise shell, pearl oyster, and cowrie shell. (Rasakalpa 5.40)
Guñjā, ṭaṅkaṇa, honey, clarified butter, and molasses constitute the five liquefiers. (Rasārṇava 5.41)
O Dear One, glass (kāca), borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), and black salt (sauvīra) constitute the triad of purifiers.
All alkaline substances remove impurities; all acidic substances are awakening agents; poisons destroy darkness [of ignorance]; and unctuous substances produce softness. (Rasaka 5.43)
Thus have the groups of medicinal herbs been described, which grant success in the union with mercury;
through their application, the powers and the great essences perform their respective functions.
Tell me that, O Goddess of Gods; what else do you wish to hear? (Ras 5.45)
The Sixth Chapter: Determination of the Characteristics and Purification of Abhraka and Other Substances.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, O Mahādeva, what are the characteristics of the powers (śaktis)?
Since it is fit for the process of extraction, let its purification be described. (Rasakalpa 6.1)
The illustrious Bhairava said: Once, when the goddess Girijā beheld Hara’s captivating form, she released her vital energy (*vīrya*); from that was born auspicious *abhraka*.
Yellow, black, white, and likewise red arise from contact with the earth. (Rasāyana 6.2)
Listen now to [the description of] mica, magnetite, diamond, and vaikrāntaka. (Ras_6.3)
The Pināka, Dardura, Nāga, and Vajra—these are the four kinds of clouds.
When fire has entered the Pināka cloud, there arises a crackling sound like "ciṭi-ciṭi."
When the frog has entered the fire, the sound becomes like that of a cock;
but when the serpent has entered the fire, O Goddess, it emits hissing breaths. (Rasārṇava 6.5)
But when the thunderbolt has entered the fire, O beloved, it remains as a thunderbolt.
Pināka and Abhra cause leprosy; Dardura brings about death;
and Nāga, when present in the body, constantly causes disease and fistula-in-ano. (Rasārṇava 6.7)
O beloved, vajra-abhraka (diamond-like mica) should be employed in both alchemy and elixirs;
that abhraka is of four kinds according to its various color variations.
One should always avoid red and yellow [minerals] for the purpose of gold, black [minerals] for those with golden bodies, white [minerals] for the work of silver, and glassy dross. (Rasārṇava 6.9)
O leader of the gods, previously, the mica was made into a single leaf with the water of *agasti* flowers and the juice of white water-lilies. *Rasārṇava 6.10*
With *kapittha*, *induka*, *jambīra*, *meghanāda*, and *punarnavā*;
with *yavaciñcā*, sour *ranāla*, *karavīra*, and red *utpala*. (Rasakalpa 6.11)
With *vanasūraṇa*, *bhūdhātrī*, *bhiṇḍīmūla*, and *amlavetasa*;
with *meṣaśṛṅgī*, rabbit fat, *śṛṅgataila*, and the juice of *śamī*. (Rasakalpa 6.12)
O Goddess, one should subject it to sudation for three days with *vajravallī*, *kṣīrakanda*, black pepper, and *sumukha*; thus it becomes free from defects. (Rasāyana 6.13)
Having first made the mica as fine as butter, one should take thirty palas of powdered mica and two palas of small fish. (Rasārṇava 6.14)

One pala of sesame powder, three palas of guñjā, and one-quarter part of ṭaṅkaṇa; this mass, bound with wheat and processed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), [is prepared]. (Rasakalpa 6.15)
Through smelting in a crucible furnace with bellows and a fierce fire, the essence of abhraka and indeed all other essences fall out. (Rasārṇava 6.16)

It should be repeatedly processed with the decoction of sudorific herbs, repeatedly subjected to *puṭapāka* (sealed heating), and then killed by means of fivefold *nicula* leaf-packets, along with a large quantity of *potaka*. (Rasārṇava 6.17)
Having applied a massed, moistureless, stainless *sattva* [of mercury] to the void,
with *umā* fruits and flowers soaked in sour *ṣaṣṭika* rice,
it clearly flows away through the churning of the *aumadaṇḍa*. (Rasārṇava 6.18)
Having placed agnijāra in a new jar, supported by a base, the sky quickly melts, possessing a luster like that of a pearl. (Rasārṇava 6.19)
O Goddess, the powder of *kañcukī* processed a hundred times and saturated with the juice of *kañcukī* will liquefy *gagana* as well as all metallic ores. (Rasārṇava 6.20)

Having been kept overnight in fermented grain-water (dhānyāmlaka) and then placed in water containing the alkaline juice of the *nicula* tree, it attains a liquid state that resembles something devoid of taste or flavor. (Rasāyana 6.21)
Having ground it with the juice of *agastya* flowers upon a *sūraṇa* tuber, and having placed it in a storage vessel buried in the earth for one month, it becomes similar to mercury. (Rasārṇava 6.22)
O Goddess, when mica is sprinkled with goat’s urine and sown with the powder of *kapitinduka* seeds, it becomes as clear as water. (Rasārṇava 6.23)
The powder of mica rubbed with the powder of *kākinī* seed and sprinkled with the milk of *snuhī* for seven days will become liquefied when heated. (Rasārṇava 6.24)
The five parts of Apāmārga and mica, well-ground together, should be placed in an earthen vessel; it will become like water. (Rasāyana 6.25)
Powdered abhraka that has been rubbed together with *kapālī* and black pepper, or sown with *śilā*, should again be combined with the juice of *agastya*. (Rasārṇava 6.26)

One should rub [the mercury] with the juice of *mārjārapādī* and sour fruits and roots, place it inside a *mātuluṅga* fruit, and bury it in the midst of rice; joined with mica and rock salt, it will liquefy in just a fortnight. (Rasakalpa 6.27)

Having placed [the ingredients] together in a single vessel for seven days, one should immerse them in the juice of *muni*, mixed with *dārvī* and black pepper, and thoroughly saturated with the juice of *maurvī*. (Rasakalpa 6.28)
Sulfur combined with Sauvarcala salt and saturated with the juice of Vajravallī, when heated in a closed crucible (śarāvasampuṭa), becomes as white as water. (Rasakalpa 6.29)
Equal parts of the powder of *vegāphala* and the dust of mica, having been processed with the milk of the *kuliśa* plant, melt instantly when heated. (Rasārṇava 6.30)
Having ground *vyoma* (mica) together with *sauvarcala* salt using the juices of *vajravallī*, one should cook it in earthen saucers;
it will melt like water. (Rasārṇava 6.31)

Furthermore, with beef, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *arka*, combined with the water of a sage (*muni-toya*) and placed inside a plantain bulb, it shall liquefy in three days over a cow-dung fire. (Rasārṇava 6.32)
Having taken a leaf of black aśmantaka, one should smear it with *pīlu* oil;
heated in the sun for seven days, it should then be placed in sour gruel for three days. (Rasārṇava 6.33)
Vajrārka, citrakakṣāra, tumbīkṣāra, likewise arjuna, sarjakṣāra, yavakṣāra, and ṭaṅkaṇa shall be the eighth. (Rasāyana 6.34)

One should apply a plaster consisting of the juice of *kṣīrakanda* and likewise the juice of *vajrakanda*, combined with the three types of *vṛhatī* and the group of alkaline substances (*kṣāravarga*). (Rasakalpa 6.35)
That mica-leaf, smeared with this paste, when heated in a bronze vessel for three days by means of blowing and exposure to the sun's heat, becomes liquefied. (Rasārṇava 6.36)
Alternatively, one should soak a leaf of mica within the milk of the *kañcukī* plant until it becomes a powder. (Rasārṇava 6.37)
One should cause thin leaf-like pieces [of the metal] to be soaked in sour liquid for three days;
then, one should smear them with that paste and place them in a brass vessel.
Through the heat of the sun for seven days, liquefaction occurs instantly. (Rasārṇava 6.38)
The powder of mica combined with the powder of *kākāṇḍī* fruit and the five fluxes, when placed in a crucible and heated, melts. (Rasārṇava 6.39)
The magnet is of four kinds: the attractor (*bhrāmaka*), the embracer (*cumbaka*), the drawer (*karṣaka*), and likewise the liquefier (*drāvaka*); the fifth is the *romakānta*. (Rasatantra 6.40)
It has one, two, three, four, or five faces, facing in every direction; it may be yellow, black, or red, or it may consist of these three colors individually. (Rasāyana 6.41)
In due order, the deities there are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
When drunk, it is yellow and possesses the power of piercing through touch; black is best for alchemy (rasāyana);
and red-colored, O illustrious lady, is praised for the binding of mercury (rasabandha). (Rasārṇava 6.43)
The *bhrāmaka* is the lowest, while the *cumbaka* is middling, O Dear One;
the *karṣaka* is superior, O Goddess, and the *drāvaka* is the most excellent of all. (Rasāyana 6.44)
O Dear One, one should cause that iron-born *kānta* to revolve; it is the *bhrāmaka*.
O Dear One, one should kiss the *kānta* which is the *cumbaka*, and one should attract the *karṣaka*. (Rasāyana 6.45)
That which directly melts metal when combined with buttermilk becomes a flux;
that same substance, when combined with mercury, causes fissures to appear, just as hair grows from a split surface. (Rasārṇava 6.46)
The one-faced [liṅga] is the smallest; the two- or three-faced is middling;
the four- or five-faced is excellent; and the all-facing (sarvatomukha) is the most supreme. (Ras 6.47)
The *bhrāmaka* and *cumbaka* types are praised for the destruction of disease;
furthermore, the *karṣaka* and *drāvaka* types are beneficial for alchemy (*rasa*) and rejuvenation (*rasāyana*). (Ras 6.48)
O charioteer, a goad is said to be the beloved of an elephant intoxicated with rut;
having dug up the field, it should be grasped with great effort. (Ras 6.49)
O beautiful goddess, one should avoid [the substance] scattered by wind and sun;
however, the magnet situated outside should be processed with goat's blood. (Rasārṇava 6.50)
One should wrap it with a cloth smeared with goat's blood;
having enveloped it in a goat skin, one should place it on the ground as before. (Rasāyana 6.51)
Having extracted it after seven months, one should place it into a water jar.
It should always be worshipped with red flowers, red garlands, and red ointments;
when worshipped with wine and meat, it should be employed for alchemy and the elixir of rejuvenation.
When processed with goat's blood, the *bhrāmaka* becomes *cumbaka*;
by this sequential method, O Dear One, it becomes *drāvaka*. (Rasatantra 6.54)
I shall describe the purification of tin and iron, which bestows supreme happiness;
it grants bodily comfort and strength when entering the living body. (Rasāyana 6.55)
Without *kāntaloha*, mercury does not penetrate the body anywhere;
[otherwise] it would pierce and pervade it instantly, like a drop of oil upon water. (Rasārṇava 6.56)
Without mercury (sūta), the beloved [gold] is not [perfected]; without the excellent mercury, the beloved is not [perfected].
The alchemical application (prayoga) joined with both the beloved and mercury sustains the body. (Ras_6.57)
Having collected barley-alkali (yavakṣāra), one should place it in a greased vessel;
then, by means of a powder of black pepper and mica, one should form a ball. When blown upon with a blowpipe, the magnetite (kāntaloha) will melt—of this there is no doubt. (Rasārṇava 6.58)

Having ground thirty units of *cumbaka* and *kānta* with the decoction of *triphalā*, one should perform the washing with that very liquid; [additionally,] five *niṣkas* of *ṭaṅkaṇa* [should be used]. (Rasāyana 6.59)
Having placed [the substance] in a worn-out cloth and wrapped it with honey and ghee, one should keep it for a period of one month; therein, O beloved, purification occurs. (Rasāyana 6.60)
The root of *sināḍikā*, weighing ten niṣkas, should be combined and thoroughly rubbed in a mortar with a decoction of the three fruits (*phalatraya*). (Rasārṇava 6.61)
The three crucibles should be placed evenly, each measuring eight finger-breadths;
the crucible should be coated with a base of one niṣka of that [mercury]. (Rasāyanatantra 6.62)
Then, having attached the crucible to the five-faced Śiva [mold] evenly,
one should firmly bind the *khoṭaka* to the hand of the machine upon the surface of the stone slab.
Having mixed it with oil, one then obtains *kāntanāga*;
furthermore, by means of the sequential application of mica (*abhraka*), one should accomplish the precipitation of the liquefied metal. (Rasārṇava 6.64)
While the ocean of milk was being churned by the gods and asuras with Mount Mandara,
that nectar was drunk by the gods, and they attained immortality.
O Goddess, as they drank, drops fell upon the surface of the earth;
having dried, they attained the nature of vajras, possessing various colors and great power. (Rasāyana 6.66)
Certain drops arose as pure grains,
and likewise as Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras in many such ways.
They are of four kinds—white, red, yellow, and black—and consist respectively of males, females, and neuters. (Rasāyana 6.68)
Those men who are rounded, fully endowed with the [auspicious] marks, radiant, and very great, should be understood as being devoid of lines and dots. (Ras 6.69)
Those [planets] joined with lines and dots are female;
those that are triangular, broad, and long are to be known as neuter. (Ras 6.70)

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, those who possess vital strength (sattva), are endowed with power, are habituated to transmuting base metals, and quickly effect the binding of mercury, are indeed male-vajras (puṃvajra). Rasāyana 6.71.
Female diamonds produce luster in the body but possess little power; neuter diamonds are devoid of essence and painfully penetrate the metal. (Rasārṇava 6.72)
Kṣatriyas are to be avoided in all [medical] activities and especially in the work of alchemy (rasakarmaṇi); they are proclaimed to be of superior, middling, and inferior [qualities]. (Ras 6.73)
O Dear One, they are coarse, very coarse, medium, subtle, and subtler;
they are free from cracking, burning, or splitting, devoid of defects and afflictions, potent, the most excellent, stainless, and exceedingly powerful. (Rasakalpa 6.74)
In the practice of *rasāyana*, a Brahmin indeed becomes a bestower of the qualities such as *aṇiman* and so forth;
a Kṣatriya [practices] for the sake of destroying death, removing wrinkles, graying hair, and disease. (Rasāyana 6.75)
The dravyakāra and likewise the vaiśya bring firmness to the body;
the śūdra effects the alleviation of disease and the stabilization of youth. (Rasārṇava 6.76)
Eunuchs are beneficial for eunuchs, women for women, and all men are beneficial for everyone.
O beloved, according to their caste, so is their energy; according to their nature, so are their qualities;
according to their taste, so is their conduct; according to their conduct, so is their excellence;
and according to their excellence, so is their complexion—thus do the Kuliśas act.
Śyāmā, śamī, ghanarava, vaṣā, mattakodrava, ākhukarṇī, munitaru, kulattha, and amlavetasa; 6.79.
O Goddess of the Gods, the juice of these [plants], as well as that of the *meṣaśṛṅgī* and the *sūraṇa* tuber, shall purify the *vajra* for three days; thus it attains purity. (Rasārṇava 6.80)
Ram's horn, snake bone, tortoise shell, bitumen, the milky sap of the snuhī plant, breast milk, and magnetite; Ras_6.81.
O Dear One, one should also place *vajraka* and *vaikrānta* in the middle of that;
having applied a *puṭa* in a fierce fire, it should remain until the end of the *puṭa* is reached. (Rasāyana 6.82)
One should grind *kulattha* and *kodrava* with horse urine and pour it onto a heated plate until it has turned to ash. (Rasārṇava 6.83)
This is the Kāpālika yoga, the supreme Vajra-slaying.
Honey, *meṣaśṛṅga*, realgar, sulphur, *kaṭaṅkaṇa*, *vaikrānta*, and *tālaka* should also be thoroughly saturated with the milk of a *vajrī* plant. (Rasārṇava 6.85)
Having applied a coating inside the crucible, one should cause it to be rotated evenly;
there the diamonds are killed and properly joined in pairs.
Grind together sulfur, realgar, the mouth of a *bhrāmaka* stone, and the teeth of a rabbit with *vetasāmla*. (Rasārṇava 6.87)
One should apply this proven medicinal paste as a coating to the crucible;
when heated within a sealed crucible (andhamūṣā), the diamond is killed in an instant. (Rasārṇava 6.88)
By that very [process], the vajra is combined with silver and gold; of this there is no doubt.

Talc, sulfur, magnetite, pyrite, camphor, borax, the stone of the tamarind fruit, ram’s horn, and menstrual blood, when ground together and applied as a coating to a crucible, cause even diamond to die (be reduced to ash) in an instant when heated. (Rasārṇava 6.90)
Then, the five parts of the *śarapuṅkha* plant should be ground with menstrual blood;
alternatively, the seed of the *peṭārī* should be ground with rice-water. (Rasāyana 6.91)
Alternatively, one should grind three karṣas of cotton root with rice-water, or grind the root of the *āraktarākā* plant with breast milk. (Rasāyana 6.92)
O observer of excellent vows, one should grind either *vajrakanda* or [other ingredients] with the milk of a *vajrī* cow;
when that paste is applied as a coating and heated, even a diamond becomes reduced to ashes.
O virtuous lady, let [the mercury] be processed for one day in a white oyster shell from the Mahānadī river with the milk of uttaravāruṇī and this paste. (Rasārṇava 6.94)
Encased in *tāla*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, and *vajravallī*, and heated within a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), the diamond (*vajra*) dies in an instant. (Ras 6.95)
O Goddess, one should place the diamond into the middle of the beloved's paste;
O Sovereign Lady, one should grind it with fragrant oil, and the diamond is killed. (Rasārṇava 6.96)

Vajra, when sprinkled with the water of horse gram (kulattha) mixed with ferrous sulfate (kāsīsa), barium sulfate (saurāṣṭrī), yellow orpiment (tālaka), and the alkali of apāmārga, becomes dead (mṛta). (Rasārṇava 6.97)

The *vajra* placed within a *meṣaśṛṅga* (sheep-horn) vessel, wrapped with the root of *amṛtā*, *timira*, seed-skin, and milk, and coated with clay, is killed by means of *puṭa* applications. (Rasārṇava 6.98)
Peṭārī, haṃsapādī, vajravallī, and sūraṇa, along with the sprouts of the aśvattha tree, O Goddess—all these should be ground together with breast milk. (Rasakalpa 6.99)
A *bṛhatī* fruit wrapped in this prepared paste (*siddhakalka*), placed [in a crucible] and coated on the outside with clay, is killed by seven *puṭa* firings. (Rasārṇava 6.100)
O Goddess, when the diamond is wrapped with white moon-streaked flowers, water, the three fragrances, and honey, it becomes dead through the process of *puṭapāka*. (Rasārṇava 6.101)
Having ground together *aśvattha*, jujube (*badarī*), *bhiṇḍī*, honey, and the shell of a crab with the milky sap of *snuhī*, a Brahmin will die from a single *puṭa* application. (Rasārṇava 6.102)
Meṣaśṛṅga, together with realgar, the milky sap of *karavīra* and *arka*, and combined with *udumbara*, when subjected to *puṭapāka*, serves for the killing of a Kṣatriya. (Rasārṇava 6.103)
Bālā, cātibalā, sulphur, and crab-shell, when processed by means of uttaravāruṇī milk and subjected to puṭapāka, result in the killing of base metals (vaiśya). Ras 6.104.
By means of *kaṇḍūla*, *sūraṇa*, *śilā*, and garlic, or with the milk of the *nyagrodha* and *śaṅkhadugdha*, even a Śūdra dies in an instant. (Rasārṇava 6.105)
By means of many large folds, thick fruits and the like are destroyed;
they become as if well-steamed, and softness arises. (Rasakalpa 6.106)
Having ground the five parts of *āmalaka* and the white *indravāruṇī*, a diamond wrapped with this [mixture] is killed by seven *puṭa* applications. (Ras 6.107)
One should place a vajra in the midst of *mātṛvāhaka* and mercury;
O Goddess, after three days of heating in a cradle (*dolāsveda*), it becomes equal to *guṇapattra*. (Rasakalpa 6.108)
O Goddess, one should place the *vajra* within an *eraṇḍa* tree;
when one month has passed, O Goddess, it becomes equal to a leaf of *guṇa*. (Rasāyana 6.109)
O Goddess, one should place the vajra in the midst of the paste of kānta, together with cotton, neem leaves, and badarī leaves. (Rasāyana 6.110)
