One should grind that [substance] together in one place, wrap it in a beautiful ball-shaped cloth, and place it between the knees, covered on the outside with a betel leaf. (Rasāyana 6.111)
Within two watches (yāma), that vajra certainly becomes soft;
at that very moment, the vajra dies within the *tārā* [mineral] and gold—of this there is no doubt. (Rasāyana 6.112)
Placed within the pulp of a citron fruit and enclosed in a cloth pouch, one should boil it in a decoction of *kodrava* grain for three days according to this sequence;
that *vajra* then becomes a solidified mass (*khoṭa*) and instantly merges with gold. (Rasāyana 6.113)
Anointed with *nāgavallī* and wrapped in its own leaf, it will certainly become soft after staying between the knees for one watch (three hours). (Ras 6.114)
At the base of the vajra-creeper, one should place a soft vajra; one should apply a seal with great care, and it will be reduced to ashes in that very instant. (Rasāyana 6.115)
For it quickly releases the being from bondage due to pleasure at that very moment;
they are the pacifiers of all death and the bringers of all accomplishments. (Rasāyana 6.116)
Having placed a pierced vajra within a chain of bones and heated it in a water-vessel for seven days, it will attain a liquid state. (Rasārṇava 6.117)
Having added the three alkalis, asafoetida, sour chickpeas, and sour vetasa, along with the milk of *jvālāmukhī* and the juice of the flesh of *sthalakumbhī*, [one should cook it]. (Rasārṇava 6.118)

O Goddess, when the vajra has been processed with these [substances] as well as the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, one should subject it to sudation in a dolāyantra; thus it becomes like mercury. (Rasakaumudī 6.119)
Alternatively, even abhraka that has been steamed, as well as pearl, coral, mākṣika,
blue-flowered [mineral], yellow [mineral], great emerald,
lapis lazuli, crystal, and so forth, dissolve like water. (Rasārṇava 6.120)
Likewise, when the metallic substance is blown [in a furnace] until it appears the color of fire, if it is cast once with a single [reagent], it becomes dead [metal] like water. (Rasārṇava 6.121)
Pearl, having been processed for seven days with *vetasāmla* (acidulated juice of *vetasa*) and placed inside the interior of a *jambīra* fruit, should be buried in a heap of grain;
by means of *puṭapāka* (sealed heating), that powder becomes like water. (Rasakalpa 6.122)
Listen, O highly fortunate goddess, to the great mercury known as vaikrānta. (Ras 6.123)
The lord of the Daityas, Mahiṣa, who had attained perfection and was born from the body of Hara,
was crushed by the goddess Bhagavatī Durgā with her trident.
Wherever his blood fell upon the earth and remained there,
in each of those places there appeared the great mineral vaikrānta, which has the form of a diamond.
It exists on the southern side of the Vindhya mountains and not at all to the north;
because it cuts through metals, it is known as vaikrāntaka.
White, yellow, red, blue, and the color of a pigeon;
another like the crest of a peacock, and one with the luster of emerald. (Rasāyana 6.127)
Vaikrānta is of seven kinds: black for the attainment of the body; yellow when [the goal] is yellow; white when [the goal] is white;
red for the granting of all success; likewise, that which has the luster of emerald;
and the remaining two are fruitless and should be avoided. Thus is vaikrānta of seven types. (Rasakalpa 6.128)
O Goddess, in whatever field the vaikrānta is situated, there the best of practitioners, having worshipped Bhairava and Vināyaka, should take it. (Rasārṇava 6.129)
Vaikrānta, finely ground into powder and honored by gods and demons, should be placed within the core of a *vyāghrī* root, heated in a crucible, and then left to cool. (Rasārṇava 6.130)
One should heat it with horse urine over a mild fire for seven days, and then dry it in the shade; this is the most excellent vaikrānta. (Rasārṇava 6.131)
Alternatively, one should subject it to fuming with salt, alkali, urine, sour liquids, and black oil, along with a decoction of *kulattha* and *kodrava*, for seven days. (Rasārṇava 6.132)
One should powder vaikrānta together with an equal portion of vandhyā powder;
having processed it with goat’s urine, one should dry it in the shade. Then, by blowing it in a closed tube (andhanāla), the essence of the crucible (mūṣāsattva) is produced. (Rasārṇava 6.133)
It should be processed with the alkali of *mokṣa*, *moraṭa*, and *pālāśa* along with cow's urine, combined with the paste of the root-tuber of *vajrakanda*, lac, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*. (Rasakalpa 6.134)
A powder produced from vaikrānta, combined with the juice of meṣaśṛṅgī and formed into a ball, when heated in a mūka-mūṣā crucible, releases its essence. (Rasārṇava 6.135)

One should grind vaikrānta and vajrakanda with the juice of the thunderbolt (vajravāri), then form it into a mass with buffalo butter and honey. Having purified it, one should blow upon it in the furnace; the essence will fall down, resembling an indragopa insect.
O Goddess, by means of sweating, *ketakī* juice, *kāṅkṣī*, and *maṇimanthaka* along with *sakhacara*, *vaikrānta* is produced, which resembles mercury in its properties. (Rasārṇava 6.137)
Gold, silver, copper, or the dust of magnetite—by this method of heating, they melt like water. (Rasārṇava 6.138)
Thus has been stated the characteristics and other qualities of the four [substances] beginning with abhraka.
Tell me that, O Goddess of Gods; what else do you wish to hear? (Rasāyana 6.139)

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Characteristics and Purification of Abhraka and Other Substances," in the *Rasārṇava*, the compendium on alchemy, within the dialogue between the illustrious Pārvatī and Parameśvara.
[The Determination of the Characteristics and Purification of Major and Minor Metals, Iron, Gems, Melting, and Killing] The Illustrious Goddess said:
Together with the characteristics and the preparations, O Great Lord, command the great elixirs,
as well as anything else of a similar nature that assists in the science of alchemy.
Śrī Bhairava said: Mākṣika, vimala, śaila, capala, rasaka,
sasyaka, darada, and srotoñjana— these are the eight [minerals].
And likewise, there are eight great tastes; listen first to these. (Rasāyana 7.2)
But Kṛṣṇa, having heard the *Bhārata*, had fallen into yogic sleep;
his sole was pierced by a hunter who mistook him for a deer. (Ras 7.3)
Those drops of blood that fell there upon the ground from the wound became, indeed, honey-stones shaped like nimba fruits. (Ras 7.4)
Among these, *mākṣika* is of two kinds, distinguished by its yellow and white varieties;
*vimala*, O Goddess, is of three kinds: white, yellow, and red. (Rasatantra 7.5)

O lady of excellent complexion, one should repeatedly subject pure *mākṣika* (honey-gold) to sudation while it is placed within a *śūraṇa* bulb, using oil, sour gruel, buttermilk, cow urine, the juice of plantain, and decoctions of *kulattha* and *kodrava*. (Rasārṇava 7.6)
Combined with alkali, sour substances, salt, castor oil, and ghee, it should be subjected to three *puṭapāka* treatments; by that, the two [substances] become purified. (Rasakalpa 7.7)
Honey-powder, processed with breast milk and the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, releases its essence when well-heated, having been treated with *ṭaṅkaṇa* and *kaṅkuṣṭha*. (Rasārṇava 7.8)
Mākṣika mineral, when saturated with plantain-root, tulasī, and sour orange,
provided with seven layers of each and combined with the five liquefiers,
and then blown upon while moistened with breast milk, releases its essence. (Rasārṇava 7.9)
Honey, gandharva-oil, cow’s urine, ghee, and the essence of the root of the plantain tree— mākṣika [sulphur] repeatedly impregnated with these, when heated in a crucible,
releases a soft essence resembling copper. (Rasārṇava 7.10)
Having added the juice of *devadālī* along with one-fourth part of borax, and having prepared an open crucible (*mūṣikā*), one should blow [the fire] to obtain the desired essence. (Rasakalpa 7.11)

What is there to marvel at here? A well-cooked *sūraṇa* tuber, placed within a casket of plantain pulp and heated by means of a *puṭa* of *vātāri* oil, attains excellent purification when burnt by the *puṭa* process. (Rasārṇava 7.12)

Cow’s urine, milk of the *snuhī* plant, and castor oil should be used to saturate [the substance] for one day; then, having ground it with honey and formed it into pills, one should sublimate the essence (*sattva*) like that of mica. This same procedure applies to *sasyaka* as well. (Rasārṇava 7.13)
Tāpya, āvartaka, dhātumākṣika, and madhudhātuka are synonyms for mākṣika.
Mākṣika is bitter and sweet; it cures urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, consumption, and skin diseases.
It alleviates kapha and pitta, is strengthening, acts as a vehicle for other drugs, and is a rejuvenative elixir. (Rasakalpa 7.14)
Since even fevers, derangements of the humors (*saṃnipāta*), and poverty perish by the mere mention of its name,
who would not employ this "piercer of metals" (*lohavedhakara*) that extends its power for a hundred *yojanas*?
[One should purify] the pure [mercury] with the juice of *śigru*, along with *kāṅkṣī*, *kāsīsa*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
Combined with *vajrakanda* and processed with the juices of plantain, it should be cultivated. (Rasāyana 7.16)
When combined with the juice of *mokṣaka* and heated in a *mūka-mūṣā* crucible, the essence (*sattva*) undoubtedly yields a substance resembling the moon and the sun. (Rasāyana 7.17)
O Īśvarī, the *śaila* is of two kinds: fallen (*patita*) and unfallen (*apatita*).
This is proclaimed in other texts as well, and it has been celebrated by many gods. (Rasārṇavasudhākara 7.18)
In the summer heat, the mountains, scorched by the sun, release their mineral essence and resin; that is celebrated as *śilājatu*. (Rasakalpa 7.19)
Like stone, the mineral ore is smelted; it is born of stone and produced from mountain peaks.
It is born of "jatu" and born of the mountain; for you have proclaimed that "giri," "śaila," and "śaila" are synonyms for mountain. (Rasārṇava 7.20)
Śilājatu is purified by being heated with alkaline, acidic, cow’s urine, or water;
alternatively, it may also be purified with cow’s ghee or with the juices of triphalā and fresh ginger.
Having placed it in an iron vessel, one should purify it with great care. (Rasāyana 7.21)
Having pulverized a mountain with grains, alkalis, and poisons, one should fashion a ball according to the prescribed rite and cause it to fall like a fickle thing. (Rasāyana 7.22)
Yellow, white, reddish, black, and fickle are praised;
however, those with a golden luster and a star-like brilliance are especially effective for binding mercury. (Rasāyana 7.23)
The remaining two middle types are like lac in that they melt quickly, yet they are fruitless;
because it melts in fire like tin, it is therefore called *capala*. (Rasārṇava 7.24)
If one binds the *capala* with a cloth and it leaps across the ocean, and the cloth immediately wraps around [the vessel], by that it is known as *capala*. (Ras_7.25)
One should refine the volatile mercury by means of *puṭapāka* on a mountain peak;
it certainly effects the binding of the body and, in particular, the binding of the mercury. (Rasārṇava 7.26)
The *capala* (calamine) that is unstable produces an unstable flux like a dense cloud;
it is considered to be a softening agent (*lekhana*), unctuous (*snigdha*), and a promoter of bodily luster and strength.
Rasaka is of three types, distinguished as earthen, molasses-like, and stone-like. (Rasaka 7.28)
That which is yellow and has the appearance of clay is the best type of clay;
that which resembles molasses is to be known as middling; and that which resembles stone is the lowest. (Ras 7.29)
Having stirred it with the exudation of *kaṭukālābu*, one should cook the mercury;
thus purified and freed from defects, it becomes yellow in color. (Rasakalpa 7.30)

What is surprising in this? Mercury, when processed with the juice of a menstruating woman and infused with flowers, and then sequentially treated with snake-venom and colored by *tripuṭa*, turns copper into gold. (Rasārṇava 7.31)
Nor does that which is of the nature of pure essence (sattva), possessed of great power, perish even when situated within the fire.
Having powdered the *rasaka* and bound it in cloth, the wise one should place it in the urine of women for seven nights, O Goddess of the Gods. (Rasaka 7.33)
One should saturate it with the juices and leaves of red and yellow flowers.
Rasaka should be repeatedly processed with alkaline substances, fats, and acids, combined with wool, lac, turmeric, harītakī, and the smoke of *bhūlatā*. (Rasakalpa 7.35)
When heated in a closed crucible (mūkamūṣā) together with borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), it undoubtedly releases an essence that resembles mercury (kuṭila). (Rasāyanasāstra 7.36)
Gobhadra, rasakastuttha, kṣitikiṭṭa, and rasodbhava are synonyms for kharpara;
it is the enemy of eye diseases and is used to color brass and copper. (Rasārṇava 7.37)
Rasa is coloring, parching, wind-increasing, and phlegm-destroying;
however, that sattva [of rasa] destroys the three doṣas and cures disorders of the eyes. (Rasakalpa 7.38)
Having drunk the kālakūṭa poison, that Garuḍa was unable to endure it;
likewise, having swallowed even the nectar, he vomited it out.
When the poison had emerged from his beak, it became that black gem known as the sasyaka.
One should soak its powder once in cow urine or in the blood of a rabbit for one day. (Rasārṇava 7.40)
O Maheśānī, one should place its powder, combined with *pādasaubhāgya*, within *karañja* oil for one day. (Rasārṇava 7.41)
One should blow upon the blind crucible while it is at the middling stage until three "cuckoo" stages have passed;
then a beautiful essence, resembling an *indragopaka* insect, falls out. (Rasārṇava 7.42)
Therefore, when the mineral is smelted in a single manner, it falls down free from blackness (kālikā), red in color, and resembling the throat of a peacock. (Rasāyana 7.43)

Sasyaka and mayūratuttha act as stimulants for the digestive fire and destroy [the effects of] time; they are suitable for rejuvenation therapy (rasāyana) and bring about the stabilization of youth. (Rasakalpa 7.44)
Sasyaka attains purity when processed with the red group of minerals.
Cinnabar (darada) is said to be of three kinds: carmāra, śukatuṇḍaka, and haṃsapāda as the third; each subsequent one possesses superior qualities.
Furthermore, mercury-cinnabar (darada) is of two kinds, distinguished as powdered and liquid mercury.
Having cooked each one—cow meat, buffalo urine, curd, sour gruel, sesame oil, and peacock bile—for three days, one should then saturate it with peacock bile. (Rasakalpa 7.48)
One should cause cinnabar to fall into a water reservoir using a *pātanāyantra*;
a metallic essence (*sattva*) resembling mercury is produced, of this there is no doubt. (Rasārṇava 7.49)
Laghukandarasa, mleccha, hiṅgula, cūrṇapārada, maṇirāgaja, and carmāragandhika are indeed synonyms for this [substance]. (Rasakalpa 7.50)
Cinnabar (hiṅgula), which is born from mercury and sulfur, is divine, bitter and hot;
it removes diseases of iron and leprosy, and it is divine for increasing strength, intellect, and digestive fire. (Rasāyana 7.51)

What is surprising in this? Darada, well-processed many times with milk, goat’s urine, and groups of sour substances, and then heated repeatedly in fire, turns white gold into the actual luster of excellent saffron. (Rasārṇava 7.52)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the *srotoja* [antimony] has the shape of an anthill’s peak; when broken, it has the luster of a blue lotus, but when rubbed, it has the hue of red chalk.
When repeatedly processed in cow dung, juice, urine, clarified butter, honey, and fat, that [mercury] quickly binds the essence of mercury (sūtaka). (Rasārṇava 7.54)
Thus the major minerals (mahārasas) have been described; now listen, O beloved, to the description of the minor minerals (uparasas).
Gandhaka, tālaka, śilā, saurāṣṭrī, khaga, gairika, rājāvarta, and kaṅkuṣṭha are known as the eight minor minerals (uparasas). (Rasakalpa 7.56)
O Goddess, in former times, on the delightful shore of the Ocean of Milk in Śvetadvīpa— which was adorned with all kinds of jewels and filled with everything that fulfills every desire— Ras_7.57.
[He was honored] by the foremost Vidyādharīs, by women,
by beloved Siddha-women, and likewise by hosts of Apsarases.
O beloved, in the past you sported with other celestial nymphs through various songs, dances, and diverse kinds of instrumental music. (Ras 7.59)
As you were thus sporting, dust was emitted from you;
that dust, O lady of beautiful hips, was exceedingly fragrant and most enchanting.
Due to the excessive abundance of dust, her garment turned red;
having cast off that garment there, she bathed well in the Ocean of Milk.
Surrounded by celestial nymphs and accompanied by the gods, you went to the city;
meanwhile, your silken garment was carried away by the waves into the midst of the ocean.
Thus, O blessed lady, your blood entered the Ocean of Milk;
during the churning of the milk-ocean, it emerged together with the nectar, gladdening all those gods and dānavas with its own fragrance. (Ras 7.63)
Then the hosts of gods said, "Let this one be named Gandhaka."
"May this [process] serve for the binding and the digestion of mercury;
may all those qualities which have been proclaimed for pārada likewise exist here. (Rasāyana 7.65)
Thus it was spoken of old by the delighted hosts of gods, O Queen of the Suras;
therefore, this substance is renowned on the face of the earth by the name Gandhaka. (Rasārṇava 7.66)
And that [mercury], O Goddess, is also of three kinds: the best is like the beak of a parrot;
the middling is yellow in color; and the lowest is white in color, my dear.
Having melted [the substance] with the oil of *karañja* and *eraṇḍa* in goat's milk, one should sprinkle it three times each upon the exudation of the *unmatta* plant. (Rasakaumudī 7.68)
One should saturate [the substance] with the powder of the *jvālinī* seed and the bile of fish, or with the juice of *bhṛṅga*, for seven days; then it should be washed with water. (Rasārṇava 7.69)
Heated over jujube charcoal in an iron vessel smeared with ghee, it is then rolled back and forth over a cloth soaked in ghee upon a gentle fire. (Rasāyana 7.70)
Gandhaka, washed quickly in the exudate of *bhṛṅga*, is beneficial. (Rasakalpa 7.71)
For sulphur is by its very nature and essential form of the nature of mercury;
one should purify the sulphur in milk as well as in the juice of ginger. (Rasāyana 7.72)
When purified seven times with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* and likewise with the juice of *nimbuka*, sulfur becomes stainless. (Rasāyana 7.73)
Tālaka (copper sulfate) is of two kinds: *paṭala* and *piṇḍa*; of these, the former is superior.
A wise person should subject *kuṣmāṇḍa* (gourd) to sudation with *tālaka* one hundred times. (Rasārṇava 7.74)

Having processed it seven times separately with the juices of *snuk*-milk, *kaṭukālābu*, sesame, mustard, *śigru*, lac, salt, jaggery, and borax, the *tālaka* (mica) will melt in an earthen crucible (*bhūdhara*). (Rasārṇava 7.75)
The wise practitioner should then grind *vyādhighāta*, *phalaksāra*, and *madhukuṣmāṇḍaka* with juices produced from *punarnavā* for seven days.

Having added all the foot-portion (one-fourth) to the dropping apparatus, one should apply the "elephant-shaped" (*gajākāra*) *puṭa* roast; then the essence will fall from the *sutālaka*. (Rasārṇava 7.77)
A red stone, cooked with beef and citron juice, should then be processed by saturation with the juices and bile of plants that have red and yellow flowers. (Rasakalpa 7.78)
It is white, black, from Saurāṣṭra, and consists of powdered fragments. (Rasakalpa 7.79)

Then, one should saturate saurāṣṭrī a hundred times with cow-bile; having blown it [into a crucible], one should precipitate the essence, which is an exceedingly secret transmuting agent. (Rasāyana 7.80)
O Dear One, green vitriol (kāsīsa) is of three kinds: white, black, and yellow. (Rasāyana 7.81)
Having powdered green vitriol (kāsīsa), one should repeatedly saturate it with the juice of *kāsamarda*, with the decoction of *rājakośātakī*, and with bile. (Rasārṇava 7.82)
Gairika is of three kinds, distinguished as red, golden, and simple; one should separately saturate it with the juices, decoctions, and bile of the red group of drugs. (Rasārṇava 7.83)
By this sequential method, one should smelt pure red ochre; gradually, the beautiful essence falls down, white and red. (Rasāyana 7.84)
O Goddess, rājāvarta is of two kinds, distinguished by its forms as a pill and as a powder. (Rasārṇava 7.85)
O Goddess of the gods, one should cook that powder in an iron vessel, mixed with buffalo milk and combined with cow’s ghee.
O Goddess of the Suras, that powder, mixed with kunaṭī and ghee, should be made into a ball using the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) along with auspicious substances;
when heated with charcoal from the khadira tree, it releases a beautiful essence. (Rasārṇava 7.87)
Kaṅkuṣṭha has the luster of coral, O beloved, and it consists of the essence (sattva).
With the juice of *sūryāvarta* roots, water-drops, *vahni*, and *śigru* roots;
with the essence of the tuber of the plantain (*kadalī*), and with the juices of *vandhyā* and *kośātakī*. (Rasārṇava 7.89)
Likewise, by means of the juices of *kākamācī*, *devadālī*, and *vajrakanda*—
either used individually or all together— along with alkalis, acids, fats, and rock salt,
the great minerals (*mahārasa*) and secondary minerals (*uparasa*) attain purification when processed (*bhāvita*). (Rasāyanasūtra 7.90)
Lac, salt, saubhāgya, the essence of incense (dhūmasāra), the three pungents, the root of śigru, beeswax, harītakī, guggulu, and the minerals. (Rasāyanasūtra 7.91)
Combined with the exudate of *sarjikā* and *sarja*, oil-cake, and *ūrṇā*, along with the five substances that cause pigeons, insects, small fish, and frogs to emerge. (Rasakalpa 7.92)
Sesame, mustard, wheat, mung beans, chickpeas, and parched grain, combined with goat’s milk, is proclaimed as *vajrapiṇḍī*. (Rasakalpa 7.93)
By means of this vajra-piṇḍī, conjoined with the five mahiṣīs, the great rasas are gladdened and purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Ras 7.94.
O lady of excellent vows, when blown upon by a fierce fire in a crucible, they release their essence;
in this same way, essence is produced from minerals, living beings, and earth. (Rasāyana 7.95)
Thus the secondary minerals (uparasas) have been described; now hear further of the metals (lohas).
Gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead—these are the six kinds of metal, and like the previous ones, they are imperishable. (Rasāyana 7.97)
In that regard, O Queen of the Gods, at the outset two metals are considered essential:
sharp iron (tīkṣṇa) and copper (śulva) for common purposes, while tin (vaṅga) and lead (nāga) are considered impure (pūtika).
Gold is born in three ways: from mercury, from the earth, and likewise from the mixture of metals; a fourth kind is not found.
O Goddess, gold is of two kinds: reddish and yellow.
When heated it is red, when cut it is white, and on the touchstone it has the luster of saffron. (Rasāyana 7.100)
Gold that is respectful (durable), soft, glossy, free from impurities such as *tāra* and copper, and enriched with sixteen colors, is recommended for both the body and metalwork. (Rasakalpa 7.101)
Clay impregnated for five days with the acidic juice of citron, along with ashes and salt, shall purify gold through the process of *puṭapāka*. (Rasārṇava 7.102)
O beloved, silver is of two kinds: white and black.
That which is heavy, glossy, soft, and white is considered the best quality of *tāra*. (Rasatantra 7.103)
Silver that has been melted with the alkali-king *nāga* seeks purification when it is cast three times into the midst of *piśācī* oil. (Rasāyana 7.104)
Copper is said to be of two kinds, O Goddess of the Gods: red and black.
That which withstands repeated hammering, is glossy, has red leaves, and is soft, is the best. (Rasārṇava 7.105)
A copper leaf smeared with the milky sap of *snuhi* and *arka*, salt, alkali, and sour substances should be immersed in the juice of *nirguṇḍī*. (Rasakalpa 7.106)
Rohaṇa, vājara, and thirdly paḍālaka—these three types of sharp iron are known as kāntaloha. (Rasārṇava 7.107)
Blue, black, glossy, consisting of fine streams, metallic, and auspicious; as well as *guḍūcī*, *haṃsapādī*, *naktamāla*, and the three fruits (*phalatraya*). (Rasaka 7.108)
Gopālaka is for the purification of dairy products, and Tumburu is for subduing iron;
one should digest these in their juices to eliminate defects in the mountain minerals. (Rasakalpa 7.109)
Tin (trapu) should be known to be of two kinds, distinguished by the difference between white and black;
that which is white, light, soft, and unctuous is called the best tin (vaṅga). (Rasāyanatantra 7.110)
But the *nāga* type, O Goddess, is of one kind: it is a swift fluxer, soft, and heavy. (Rasārṇava 7.111)
By sowing with the powder of buffalo bone and sprinkling it with its urine, tin becomes pure;
likewise, lead [becomes pure] from the bone and urine of an elephant.
Gaurī fruits, kṣuraka, turmeric, tumburu,
the seeds of kuberākṣa, and mallikā, O beautiful one— Ras 7.113.
By means of the application of the alkali of *palāśa* and dried *apāmārga*, together with the milk of *snuk*,
and by soaking it seven times, they purify the serpent.
Then, by means of the combination with the milk of *snuhī*, one should cause tin (*vaṅga*) to be infused.
With the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, the tubers of *halinī* and *kañcukī*, *citraka*, *guñjā*, *karañja*, *dhuttūra*, the root of *hayagandhā*, and *tālaka*; (Ras 7.116)

Then, by means of a bath with the roots of *naktamāla*, *iṅgudī*, *śakra*, and *vāruṇī* ground together and soaked for seven nights in buffalo buttermilk, the impurity of all metals is destroyed; of this there is no doubt. (Rasārṇava 7.117)
Gold, repeatedly impregnated with the juices of the powder of *devadālī* fruit, should be liquefied by the addition of [other substances]; it shall not become hard again. (Rasārṇava 7.118)
And by its power, one may cause all sentient beings to melt away. (Rasāyana 7.119)
O Goddess, when an equal portion of the dust of *suragopa* and *suradālī* is added, it turns the gold into something resembling water. (Rasārṇava 7.120)
By means of a post-treatment with frog-bone, fat, alum, *hayalālā*, and *indragopa* insects, gold remains in a molten state for a very long time. (Rasārṇava 7.121)
The ash of *jvālinī* should be filtered twenty-one times through cow’s urine and dried;
by sowing [the resulting powder] into it, even hard metal placed in a crucible will melt. (Rasārṇava 7.122)

By being processed twenty-one times with the ash of *nicula* and the juices of *ketakī*, even a sharp substance will attain a state of fluidity through the addition of these ingredients. (Rasārṇava 7.123)
Having been processed for seven days in the juice of ripe *dhātrī* fruits within a conch shell, it is then processed again for seven days with the water of a *kañcuki* plant. (Rasārṇava 7.124)
O Goddess of the Gods, that sharp powder, placed within a pair of shallow bowls and firmly sealed, is transformed into the form of mercury.
Copper sulfate, realgar, orpiment, honey-stone (mākṣika), red ochre, green vitriol, alum, borax, blue vitriol, and mica; // Ras_7.126 //
The excrement of a dog, a jackal, and a hyena, as well as that of a cock, along with equal parts of the feces of a peacock, a vulture, and a cat; Ras_7.127.
One should soak it three times with the milky sap of *snuhī* and the juice of *devadālī*;
then, one should smear iron leaves with that paste using one-eighth part [of the total weight]. (Rasārṇava 7.128)
One should heat [the metal] until it becomes liquid and then quench it with these very [substances].
One should grind the roots of *aṅkola* with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and apply that as a coating to the metal; then, O Dear One, one should hold it while it is situated in the fire. (Rasārṇava 7.129)
Then one should apply a coating with the juice of *paricchinnā*, O Goddess of Gods; with the bile of fish, O Beloved, one should hold it while placed in fire. (Rasārṇava 7.130)
One should again apply a coating derived from the root of *lāṅgalī*;
by three such coatings, the metal quickly becomes stainless, like clear water. (Rasārṇava 7.131)
O Goddess, powdered tortoise shell, ram horn, and bitumen, when applied as a counter-powder (prativāpa), make [the mercury] as firm as water is when possessed of strength. (Rasārṇava 7.132)
One should prepare an alkali from *arka*, *apāmārga*, *musalī*, *nicula*, as well as *citraka*, *kadalī*, *potakī*, and *dālī*. (Rasaka 7.133)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should filter it six times in buffalo urine;
by this addition, the dust produced from the essence of mica and other minerals will be liquefied. (Rasārṇava 7.134)
Just as the root of the danti plant specifically causes water to flow away, [so too does it act upon the humors].
The powder of vaikrānta, soaked in the juice of uttaravāruṇī, will cause the metals to melt like water by means of its addition as a flux. (Rasārṇava 7.136)
I shall describe the liquefaction of gems as well as the liquefaction of the sky.
Triphalā, trikaṭuka, the three alkalis (trikṣāra), the five salts (paṭupañcaka), balā, atibalā, and thirdly mahābalā. (Rasāyanasūtra 7.138)
Aśvagandhā, cavī, nārī, bhūlatā, mātṛvāhaka, gopendramaṇḍalī, ṣaḍbindu, and likewise dvimukhī. (Rasāyana 7.139)
Dhīrā, sūraṇa-kanda, kañcukī, punarnavā, snuhī, arka, unmatta, halinī, pāṭhā, and uttaravāruṇī; (Ras 7.140).
Magnetite, *gokṣura*, soft *dūrvā* grass, *amlavetasa*, bitumen (*śilājatu*), *sauvīra*, poison, sulphur, and potassium carbonate (*kaṭaṅkaṇa*). (Rasakalpa 7.141)
One should have all ten palas of each [ingredient] made into a fine powder;
[one should also prepare] two jars of horse gram (kulattha) and wood of the *tiniśa* tree. (Rasakalpa 7.142)
One should boil it over a gentle heat until only one *kumbha* remains;
with that decoction, one should saturate that powder twenty-one times. (Rasāyana 7.143)
The gems should be smeared with that [substance] and then heated while immersed in its decoction; within a day and night, they quickly liquefy like water. (Rasāyana 7.144)
Indeed, iron and other metals such as mica melt without hesitation and become stainless, resembling the seed of Śiva. (Rasāyana 7.145)
And those [mercury and gold] situated in the fire quickly unite with the essence; by merely touching those liquefied substances, mercury (sūtaka) is bound in an instant. (Rasāyana 7.146)
I shall describe the killing of metals; listen with a concentrated mind.
Vermilion, gold, and silver [are killed] with the milky sap of the *snuhī* plant. (Rasārṇava 7.147)
With that same [milk], one should process honey-copper; with goat's milk, sulfur;
with breast milk, vermilion, sharp iron (tīkṣṇa), tin, and palāśa-leaf [mineral]. (Rasārṇava 7.148)

O beloved, one should kill nāga by making it into clear leaves with the milk of *śilārka* and then applying *puṭapāka*; thus, ash is produced that is free from residue (*niruttha*). (Rasakaumudī 7.149)
There is no iron elephant that the musk-deer-maned lion, or the honey-bee-maned lion, would not slay by the mere scent [of its presence]. (Rasāyana 7.150)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, when metals have been reduced to a liquid essence (rasa), they remove all diseases; how much more so when combined with medicinal extracts!
Furthermore, through their regular practice, they utterly destroy wrinkles, graying hair, illness, and old age. (Rasārṇava 7.151)
Vajra, mākṣika, tīkṣṇa, and abhra are recommended for bodily treatments;
one should employ nāga, vaṅga, and suvīra for chemical processes. (Rasārṇava 7.152)
O Goddess, that iron which is *paribāla* and likewise that which originates from Malaya—these two types of iron, in particular, provide protection for the body. (Rasārṇava 7.153)
"Having understood the passion of the great juices and so forth, one should accomplish the seeds;
tell me that, O Goddess of Gods, what else do you wish to hear? (Ras 7.154)
8 [Seed-Syllable Sadhana] The Glorious Goddess said: "O Lord of the Gods, regarding the great essences, the metals, and the gems..."
O Lord, tell me likewise the enumeration of passion and the practice of the seed-syllable.
The illustrious Bhairava said:

O Goddess of the gods, when the defect of the mountain-mineral has been eliminated, those [substances] cause the mercury to take on a coppery redness twice as great as that found in the great minerals (*mahārasa*). (Rasāyana 8.2)
Sasyaka, capala, rājāvarta, mākṣika, vimala, and gairika—each one of these should be double [the amount of the previous]. (Rasāyana 8.3)
In desirable substances such as *bhrāmaka* and others, that [mercury] indeed possesses one, two, or three qualities;
and in each variety of mica (*abhraka*), it is white, yellow, or reddish-white.
Eighteen thousand units of mercury reside in sulphur;
ten thousand, O Goddess, in cinnabar, and two thousand in realgar. (Rasārṇava 8.5)
Seven thousand [units] are revealed for mercury, while four are for kaṅkuṣṭha;
these appear in the *rasagarbha* if the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*) takes place. (Rasaka 8.6)
One hundred and twelve plus five types of passion are established in Nāga;
one thousand minus one hundred types of passion are established in Vaṅga.
Five hundred and fifty tints are established within the copper;
and sixteen tints, red, yellow, and white, are found in gold. (Rasāyana 8.8)
O Goddess of the Gods, sixty thousand passions are established in the Śakranīla [stone],
and in the Mahānīla, those passions are established as double that amount.
O Goddess of the Gods, there are thirteen hundred thousand colors in the māṇikya;
they know the pearl (muktāphala) to be a gem produced from the water of elephants. (Rasārṇava 8.10)
Three thousand, six thousand, and nine hundred thousand varieties of redness are established in the *gaja*, the *vārijaka*, and the *padmarāga* [gems], respectively. (Rasārṇava 8.11)

O Goddess of the Gods, that which pierces all metals and yet is not pierced by anything else is known as *vajra*; its red color is understood to be two hundred thousand [times more intense]. (Rasāyana 8.12)
Sixteen thousand [beings] are established in the Puṣparāga; O Dear One, those with a color slightly less than a hundred thousand are said to be in the Marakata. (Rasārṇava 8.13)

One who does not know the calculation of passion (rāga) regarding the transmuted essence (rasa) will over-refine the metal if it is superior, or reveal it as inferior if it is deficient. (Rasāyana 8.14)
O Pārvatī, that lord of men who indeed knows how to calculate the number of passions by means of hundreds of millions,
and who likewise perceives their touch, is pierced by hundreds of millions [of darts]. (Ras 8.15)
Henceforth, O beloved, I shall explain the accomplishment of the seeds;
O Goddess, the seed is first of all of two kinds, according to gold and silver. (Rasāyana 8.16)

The seed of gold becomes [perfected] by means of yellowish-red [substances], while the seed of silver becomes so by means of white ones; thus, it further becomes threefold: prepared, colored, and matured. (Rasāyana 8.17)
And that imagined [nature] is of two kinds, through the distinction between the pure and the mixed.

O Goddess of the Gods, the preparation of the seeds of mercury, the secondary minerals (uparasa), and the metals is performed separately—whether pure or mixed through combination—according to what is available. (Rasārṇava 8.19)
Sattva, having been revolved in the sky and purified with glass and borax,
and treated with sprinklings of the paste of tamarind fruit and *nirguṇḍī* leaves,
becomes cooked and consolidated, O Goddess, fit for being ground with mercury. (Rasārṇava 8.20)

By means of the groups of fats, alkalis, and acids, and after three *puṭa* applications with realgar (*śilā*), on the day of death [of the metal], through fumigation in a *dhūpanayantra* and by the application of fragrant incense and ointments;
likewise, according to the procedure for tin (*vaṅga*) or for killed *tālaka* (orpiment). (Rasakalpa 8.21)
Alternatively, when processed with realgar and cinnabar, or with mercury, the black leaf of gold and silver will melt within the mercury-filled crucible. (Rasārṇava 8.22)
O Dear One, that which is called *saṃkara* is difficult to mix, being characterized by softness and hardness;

then, O Goddess, when it is thoroughly kneaded, there occurs a rapid union of the pair (*dvaṃdvamelāpana*), which becomes a single flavor within the womb and dissolves into the King of Mercury (*rasarāja*). (Rasārṇava 8.23)
Henceforth I shall explain the union of the pairs; listen. (Rasārṇava 8.24)
O Dear One, the powder of *varṣābhū*, plantain root, *kākamācī*, and *punarnavā*,
together with human skull, *guñjā*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*,
when well-heated with milk and oil, causes gold and mica to merge. (Rasārṇava 8.25)
By this very same procedure, one should also mix tāra-bhrām.
O Goddess of the Gods, having melted tin and again joined it with mercury, one should grind it with the juice of plantain root mixed with borax;
when heated in a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), the tin and mica merge in an instant. (Rasārṇava 8.27)
The powder of human skull, woman’s breast milk, forest *śigru*, *guñjā*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, combined with tin and mica, unite in an instant. (Rasārṇava 8.28)

Having powdered mica (abhraka) and saturated it with the juice of *kākamācī*, then treated it with the juice of *kapittha* and combined it with mercury (*rasa*) and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), one should place it between sheets of tin foil and heat it; thus, the mica and tin will merge. (Rasārṇava 8.29)
Having stirred it with pungent oil, one should add the ash of *apāmārga*, tin, mica, and yellow orpiment; however, in the case of lead-mica, one should add realgar. (Rasāyana 8.30)
Gold-colored mica is combined with lead calamine; starry mica with tin and orpiment;
copper-colored mica with sulfur; and sharp mica with Sindhu-hiṅgula.
Tin-colored mica is mixed with yellow orpiment, and lead-colored mica with realgar. (Rasaratnasamuccaya 8.31)
Lāṅgalī, the hair of a yak-tail, cotton-seed, horse-gram, bhūlatā, aśmadalanī, breast-milk, and the earthworm; Ras_8.32.
When thoroughly smelted with a fierce fire in a crucible smeared with this [substance], all the pure varieties of *kāntaloha*, mica, and mountain-ore unite in an instant. (Rasārṇava 8.33)
The flesh of the *latāchuchundarī* combined with poison and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, when used as a coating for the crucible (*mūṣā*), effects the fusion of all dual [metallic] combinations. (Rasārṇava 8.34)
Abhraka, surasā, śṛṅga, the fat of a frog, and poison—by means of a combination with guñjā and ṭaṅkaṇa, these cause paralysis in all living beings. (Rasārṇava 8.35)
All dualities are reconciled by means of ṭaṅkaṇa, wool, girija, sulphur, that which is called karṇa, amala, and karkaṭa, when these are ground together with breast milk. (Rasāyana 8.36)

In the context of rejuvenation (rasāyana), all disorders born of dual humors (dvaṃdvaja) are treated with dhātakī, guggulu, jaggery, sarja, barley-gruel, and potassium carbonate (ṭaṅkaṇa), ground together with breast milk.
The subtle powder of *khasattva*, combined with the previous paste and placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), when heated, merges with the mixture in an instant. (Rasāyanatantra 8.38)
Khasattva, when sown with tāpya, rasaka, sasyaka, and darada, becomes firmly bound; once strongly heated, it then merges [with them]. (Rasāyana 8.39)
One should melt all the mercury, secondary minerals, and metals together in one place;
they enter into mutual union and flow like water. (Rasārṇava 8.40)
Thus the seeds are prepared; now hear further about how they are dyed. (Rasāyana 8.41)
The thick [mercury] is colored with honey-powder and copper-powder; when combined with the essence of *tāpya*, it effects the coloring of the king of fluids (*rasarāja*). (Rasāyana 8.42)
With red-tinged creepers, cow's urine, and numerous infusions of realgar, sulphur, orpiment, gold-ore, and cinnabar; 8.43.
Then, having been sown with and treated by the red group of substances and oils, the mercury (rasarāja) becomes dead;
this is the process of coloring, especially when using sharp copper.
Pure, stainless copper, when treated with cinnabar, becomes tripled in weight; once digested, it yields a pure mercury with the luster of lac. (Rasārṇava 8.45)

O Īśvarī, having added twice as much mercury and well-smelted copper, one should repeatedly apply the powder of black abhraka along with the red-group substances in sealed crucibles (puṭas). Rasaka 8.46.
Or, dead gold (mercury) may be quenched three times with *tāpya* (cinnabar);
likewise, *rasaka* (calamine) combined with *tāpya* and rock salt should be placed in a crucible (*bhāṇḍikā*). (Rasakalpa 8.47)

Through double the amount of digestion (*jāraṇa*), the mercury—resembling an *indragopa* insect up to that point—becomes liquefied and takes on the appearance of gold; of this there is no doubt. (Rasāyana 8.48)
One should color mica, gold, and copper with realgar, pyrite,
the finest red ochre, and green vitriol.
Thus the seeds are indeed colored; now hear about the ripened seeds.
One should add the major and minor metallic juices as well as sharp metals, along with an equal portion of vitriol (mākṣika), through the application of sulfur and alkali. (Rasāyana 8.51)
One should grind this [substance] a hundred times; it remains unexhausted with a residue, and when combined with an equal portion of mercury, it certainly dissolves within its womb. (Rasāyana 8.52)

O Goddess of the Gods, this very [process] is recommended for the digestion (*jāraṇā*) in the "pillar of the draft-animal" (*viṣṭikā-stambha*), as well as for the coloring (*rañjana*) and the amalgamation (*sāraṇā*) of the king of mercury (*rasarāja*). (Rasārṇava 8.53)
That very [substance], when drenched hundreds of times with red-colored oils, is highly recommended for those [processes]; it acts as a penetrator (*vedhakṛt*) by a thousandfold part. (Rasāyana 8.54)
When processed with lead and tin for the purpose of gold and silver, the essence of mica (khasattva) should be combined with copper;
thus, in the form of a binary compound (dvaṃdvita), it is used in elixir therapy (rasāyana). (Rasāyanatantra 8.55)

One should cause tin and lead to be absorbed into copper by means of those juices containing oil, alkali, and the five acids, along with orpiment and other minerals, in proportions of one, two, or three times [the weight of the copper]. (Rasārṇava 8.56)
When that [substance] is sprinkled with blood and oil, it is known as "rasākarṣaṇī" (the attractor of mercury). // Ras_8.57 //

One should repeatedly process honey, sulphur, yellow orpiment, realgar, vaikrāntaka, the best of the kantis, sasyaka, vimala, añjana, and rasaka— having been sown [into a crucible] and pulverized— within gold. (Rasakalpa 8.58)

Through repeated applications of *puṭa* (herbal) roasting with iron-foil (*lohaparpaṭikā*), *tāpya*, *kaṅkuṣṭha*, *vimalā*, *abhra*, dead copper (*mṛtaśulva*), mica-essence (*śilāsattva*), the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, and *hiṅgula*, lead (*nāga*) attains the state of being lifeless (*nirjīvatā*). (Rasārṇava 8.59)

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should process mercury, realgar, conch-shell, mica, and the alkali of *ciñcā* fruit, as well as tin, dead lead, dead tin, copper, or dead iron, each individually into superior gold. (Rasārṇava 8.60)

When the etymological analysis has been thoroughly mastered by hundreds of groups, the light [of the self] resembles yellow orpiment in the sun, and resembles the color of a pearl in the moon. (Ras 8.61)
Equal parts of sharp mica and twice as much *mākṣika* ore should be melted together, powdered, and then killed by means of seven *puṭa* applications. (Rasāyana 8.62)
When the gold has been refined a hundredfold, one should digest that seed with an equal amount;
by smearing it upon the leaves of *candrārka*, it will transmute [the base metal] by means of a hundredth part. (Rasāyana 8.63)
By adding honey above and below, copper becomes equal to gold;
thus, when the seed is processed tenfold, it becomes identical to its cause. (Rasārṇava 8.64)

Then, O beloved, one should smelt mercury-calcite (rasakābhra) along with iron, magnetite, and copper in increasing proportions; once that has been killed with realgar (mākṣika), one should cause it to flow into the seed (bīja).
Having heated thirty-two times in gold, one should carry lead that has been struck;
with the addition of thirty parts of mica, it is declared to be the seed of lead (nāgabīja). (Rasaratnasamuccaya 8.66)

By adding the essence (sattva) of yellow abhraka obtained through heating and alkaline salts, one should cause this to flow into the seed; this is the penetrator (vedhaka) for that which has been processed by a woman. (Rasārṇava 8.67)
The nāga makes it soft; when processed, that softness becomes red; when sown, it becomes yellow; the sharp [variety] produces a blackish tint when placed in a beautiful vessel. (Rasārṇava 8.68)
The seed-syllable of mercury is thus declared; now hear the seed-syllable of silver.
Equal parts of sharp mica, copper, and purified cinnabar, along with four parts of tin—all of this should be smelted together and then finely powdered. (Rasakalpa 8.70)
The work killed by means of a *puṭa* should be spread out, and one should pierce the silver (*tāra*).
Thirty-two times the quality [of the base] should be applied to the silver; the killed *tāpya* should be carried into the tin (*vaṅga*).
From thirty-fold application of *tāla*, the seed of tin (*vaṅgabīja*) is declared. (Rasārṇava 8.71)
One should also cause *kuṭila* (copper), *vimala* (mica), *tīkṣṇa* (iron), and *khasattva* (mica-essence) to be processed;

or else, by means of the addition (*vāpa*) of *vaṅga* (tin), *abhra* (mica), or *tāpyasattva* (calamine essence), one should perform sprinkling with white flowers and with substances mixed with fats. (Rasārṇava 8.72)
The seed-syllables beginning with *tāra* have been stated; now hear the coloring of the seed-syllables.
One should dye the seeds with sharp *mākṣika*, copper, and killed lead, until they resemble vermilion (*sindūra*). (Rasārṇava 8.74)
Having placed the serpent (mercury) in a crucible along with the petals of the Brahma-seed (Brahmī), and having applied fire beneath it, when it becomes the color of fire; Ras_8.75.
With vāsaka, vibhītaka, śāka, kiṃśuka, and śigru;
with the flower of koraṇḍaka, and those of bakula and arjuna.

With *ahimāra*, with a female serpent (*nāginī*), with a maiden (*kumārī*), with a daughter of the *nāgas* (*nāgakanyā*), with threefold stone (*śilā*), and with goat’s urine boiled [together]. (Ras 8.77)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, having repeatedly soaked the processed [substance] placed in a skull-cup, it is killed in just seven days. (Rasāyana 8.78)
One should first envelop [the mercury] with sulphur and subsequently with acidic substances.

This is to be employed for the coloring of petals, seeds, and the king of liquids (mercury), as well as for opening [the essence], causing it to ascend, and especially for the stabilization of the paste. (Rasārṇava 8.79)
In a decoction of mañjiṣṭhā and kiṃśuka, [one should boil] khadira, red sandalwood (raktacandana), karavīra, devadāru, sarala, and the two types of turmeric (rajanīdvaya). // Ras_8.80 //
O Goddess, having ground other red flowers with lac juice, one should cook oil; with that, one should dye the seeds. (Rasāyana 8.81)
O Goddess of the Gods, one part of oil should be cooked with double the amount of red flowers, four times the amount of milk, and a decoction of the group of red and yellow substances. Rasāyana 8.82.
[The juice] derived from *jyotiṣmatī*, *karañja*, and *kaṭutumbī*, combined with the juices of *pāṭalī*, *pippalī*, *kāma*, and *kākatuṇḍī*. (Rasāyanatantra 8.83)
Combined with the fat of a frog, a pig, a ram, a snake, a fish, a tortoise, and a leech, along with sixteen parts of well-ground [substances], [this is prepared]. (Rasāyana 8.84)
This [mercury], cooked with the medicinal herbs *bhūlatā*, *mala*, *ākṣika*, and the two *melāpana* drugs, and then filtered, is called *sāraṇā-taila*. (Rasārṇava 8.85)
O Dear One, just as a seed that has reached the state of *garbhadruti* becomes equal to its essence, so too all [the elements] are held to be equal in their pervasive nature. (Rasāyana 8.86)
That which is well-cooked, excellent, and uniform within the womb should be made to flow and color that [substance]. (Rasāyana 8.87)
Having spoken thus, [the teacher said]: "One should digest these seeds through the application of *viḍa* (fecal matter).
Tell me that, O Goddess of Gods; what else do you wish to hear? (Rasārṇava 8.88)
9 [The Discourse on Excrement] The Śrī Devī said: "The formation of the seed-syllables has been proclaimed, as well as their specific means of accomplishment."
You should explain those fluxes by which these [substances] are digested and from which they are produced.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Kāsīsa, saindhava, kāṅkṣī, sauvīra, vyoṣa, gandhaka,
sauvarcala, sarjikā, and that which is produced from the juice of mālatī flowers.
This viḍa salt, sprinkled with the juices of the roots of the śigru plant, is a digestant for all [substances].
O Goddess, conch powder that has been burnt and soaked a hundred times in the milk of the sun plant (ravikṣīra),
having been subjected to many *puṭa* applications, is praised as a flux for the process of *jāraṇā*.
Or one may take sulphur that has been washed a hundred times with cow's urine and reduced to powder.
Conch powder that has been burnt and then saturated a hundred times with water from the roots of *śigru*, combined with poison and rock salt (*sindhūttha*), is called *vaḍavāmukha*. (Rasārṇava 9.5)
O Goddess, one should saturate ṭaṅkaṇa a hundred times with the juices of *kiṃśuka* flowers;
this is called *viḍa* or *vahnimukha*, which is dear for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of metals, O Beloved. (Rasārṇava 9.6)
O beloved, cūlikā, sulphur (gandhapāṣāṇa), and the mouth of magnetite—each one alone is sufficient for the digestion of iron powder. (Rasārṇava 9.7)
One should cook sulphur, yellow orpiment, rock salt, antimony, borax, realgar, and green vitriol with alkaline substances and animal urines; this is *jvālāmukha* flux (*viḍa*). (Rasārṇava 9.8)
Nicula alkali, processed twenty-one times with the juice of *devadālī* leaves, will digest all metallic essences (*sattva*). (Rasārṇava 9.9)
Vāstuka, eraṇḍa, kadalī, devadālī, punarnavā, vāsā, palāśa, nicula, tila, kāñcana, and mākṣika. (Rasakalpa 9.10)
All the parts [of the plant] should be cut into pieces on a stone slab so that they are not overly dried out;
likewise, one should take the five parts of sesame stalks and radishes. (Rasāyana 9.11)
One should saturate water with the group of urines and then filter it; knowing the proper measure of fire, one should cook it in a vessel of iron using the haṃsapāka apparatus. (Rasakalpa 9.12)
When there is the emergence of many bubbles and vapors, then [one should take] green vitriol, saurāṣṭrī, the three alkalis, and the three pungents. (Rasakalpa 9.13)
Take sulphur, white salt, asafoetida, and the six salts;

one should throw their powder into the middle of an iron crucible. After being buried underground for seven days, it should then be placed in grain; this is the excellent *viḍa* salt. (Rasakalpa 9.14)

The two types of viḍa salt should be cooked a hundred times each in succession with the sour juice of jambīra and the decoction of the root of śigru, after being sprinkled with cūlikā and sulphur. (Rasakalpa 9.15)

One should impregnate *devadālī* and *śivā* seeds, along with *guñjā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), with the juice of *koṣātakī* leaves or with alkalis derived from *nicula*; then, one should saturate this with the group of sour substances (*amlavarga*). This is *viḍa* salt, which serves for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of gold. (Rasaka 9.16)

Sulfur should be processed a hundred times with the alkaline solutions of radish, ginger, and *citrā*, strained through cow’s urine; this is *viḍa* salt, used for the digestion of gold. (Rasāyanasamhitā 9.17)
Haritāla, śilājatu, kṣāra, salt, conch-shell, and pearl-oyster shell—this mixture, when cooked by the haṃsapāka method, becomes viḍa for the digestion of gold. (Rasārṇava 9.18)
Having thus gathered the necessary materials, one should perform the process of extraction (*rasakarma*).
Tell me that, O Goddess of Gods; what else do you wish to hear? (Rasāyana 9.19)
10 [Purification of Mercury] The Śrīdevī said: What is the characteristic of mercury, and what is its activity like?
I do not know that, O Lord of Gods; you ought to explain it to me according to reality.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
The origin of mercury has already been described; now hear its characteristics. 10.2.
His names number in the thousands, tens of thousands, and even millions;
it is not possible for me to speak them all, so listen as they are told in brief. (Ras 10.3)
Rasa, rasendra, sūta, pārada, and then miśraka. (Rasakalpa 10.4)
One should know that *rasa* is perfected mercury (*siddharasa*) which takes refuge in a perfected field (*siddhakṣetra*);
it destroys all diseases as well as wrinkles and graying hair. (Ras 10.5)

Now listen to [the description of] pure mercury (rasendra), which produces strength and vitality in the body, gold, and acts as an agent in digestion (jāraṇa) and transmutation (sāraṇa). (Rasārṇava 10.6)
The mercury (sūtaka) that is slightly yellowish, has a rough body, and is possessed of impurities is [of this type]. (Rasāyana 10.7)

O Goddess, that which is white on the outside and inside, abundant and covered by a sheath— that one should know to be mercury (pārada), and one should employ it for the work of transmutation (tārakarma).
Just as a vessel of milk is destroyed by contact with sour gruel,
so too the golden body is destroyed by mercury.
The wise know that the *miśraka* type has the luster of a peacock's feather;
upon seeing mercury of a smoky color, it is specifically recognized as such.
One should understand that the *miśraka* indeed performs the function of causing [the mercury] to marry [its consort]. (Rasāyanasāra 10.9)
Thus, O Goddess, the fivefold varieties of rasa have been described. (Ras 10.10)

Sudation, rubbing, moving, digesting, liquefying, coloring, stretching, and transmuting—in this sequence; he who knows these according to their true nature, for him the elixir (sūtaka) is perfected. (Rasārṇava 10.11)
Intensity arises from sweating, and purity from rubbing;
one should produce strength through stirring, and binding occurs through digestion. (Rasārṇava 10.12)
Its unity arises from liquefaction; its redness from red ointment (*raktakāñjana*);
its pervasiveness from extraction (*sāraṇā*); and likewise, its transmissibility from transmutation (*krāmaṇa*). (Rasārṇava 10.13)
The wind moving as impurity becomes the swan-movement (haṃsaga) swiftly; the wind moving as impurity becomes the smoke-movement (dhūmaga) when accompanied by smoke. (Rasāyana 10.14)
O Goddess, there is another course for the vital principle (jīva); the vital principle may emerge as if from an egg.
It sustains the living being; therefore, the vital principle is known as "rasa" (the essence). 10.15.
His fourfold course is indeed attained through skill;
four courses are visible, while the fifth course is invisible.
Through mantra, meditation, and other such means, his fifth destiny is exhausted.
Smoking, crackling, leaping like a frog, immobility, and trembling—these are the five stages of the rasa. (Ras 10.18)
When being churned by means of a paste (kalka), three stages indeed arise:
first the stage in water (jala-gati), then the stage of impurity (mala-gati), and thereafter the stage of the swan (haṃsa-gati). (Rasārṇava 10.19)

Then, having given pure gold, one should cook that [mercury] with a stabilizer and a binding agent; having added the juice of the medicinal plant *niyāmakagaṇa*, one should cause it to digest. (Rasārṇava 10.20)
O Śivā, when restrained, it does not proceed in the manner of smoke. (Rasāyana 10.21)
Free from the movement of the *kaṇikā* and devoid of bubbles, this [mercury] becomes restrained like the fire in a cooking pot. (Rasārṇava 10.22)

O auspicious lady, when one causes the mercury to digest [the impurities] in a vessel of sour gruel (kāñjika) without having restrained it, then its threefold course certainly arises. (Rasārṇava 10.23)

O Goddess, having been certainly sweated for three days by means of the dolāsveda (swinging-sudation), the king of mercury does not diminish, even when subjected to the vasubhaṇṭa and other processes. (Rasārṇava 10.24)
Having observed that the mercury has not yet been fully exhausted, one should then add the [substances] beginning with *vyoma* (mercurial calx);
thereafter, the process of sweating (*svedana*) and the grinding (*mardana*) of the substance being administered should be performed. (Rasārṇava 10.25)
Food embraced by the *rasa* is called *piṣṭikā*;
its rapid digestion within the womb of the *rasa* is proclaimed as *jāraṇa*. (Rasārṇava 10.26)

That is declared to be *jāraṇā* (digestion), and it is perceived in this very way; at the end of digestion, the process of coloring (*rañjana*) should be performed with the group of red substances (*raktavarga*). (Rasārṇava 10.27)
When it has been repeatedly processed until it is thoroughly purified and reddened, one should cause it to flow by means of equal amounts of gold;
through the application of the *sāraṇā* apparatus, the mercury thus flowed becomes bound. (Rasārṇava 10.28)
Having repeatedly processed it so that it becomes a *sūtaka*, one should employ it in the act of piercing (*vedha*) when combined with the process of transmutation (*krāmaṇa*). (Rasārṇava 10.29)
Āroṭa is pārada and Brahmā; when swooned, it is Janārdana;
when bound, the mercury (rasa) takes the form of Rudra through the power of the yoga of action. (Ras 10.30)
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain in detail the yoga of action (karmayoga). Ras_10.31 //
Mercury has three defects: poison, fire, and impurity.

Through the poison, one should know it becomes poisonous; through the fire, a man becomes afflicted with leprosy; through the impurity, he suffers from abdominal disease; and [if these are not removed], he dies during the practice of *rasāyana*. (Ras 10.32)
Six *truṭis* make one *likṣā*, and six *likṣās* make one *yūka*;
six *yūkas*, O lady of noble vows, are said to be known as a *rajas*. (Ras 10.33)
Six *rajas* are directly a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*), and that is proclaimed as a *siddhārtha*;
and six *siddhārthas*, O Goddess of Gods, are proclaimed to be one barley grain (*yava*). (Ras 10.34)
Six *yava* make one *guñjā*, and six *guñjā* make one *māṣaka*.
Twelve *māṣa* make one *tola*, and eight *tola* make one *pala*. (Rasāyanatantra 10.35)
O Goddess, thirty-two palas are proclaimed to be one *śubha*;
two thousand *śubhas* are proclaimed to be one *bhāra*. (Ras 10.36)
Two thousand palas, or one thousand, or even just one hundred;
or twenty-eight palas, or ten, or even five. (Rasāyana 10.37)
The purification of the *sūtaka* (mercury) must be performed with exactly half a *palā*. Ras_10.38 //
O Goddess of the gods, one should cause mercury to sweat for three days using the essences of mahābalā, nāgabalā, meghanādā, punarnavā, and meṣaśṛṅgī, combined with fresh butter. (Rasārṇava 10.39)
Girikarṇī, mīnākṣī, sahadevī, punarnavā, uragā, triphalā, kāntā, laghuparṇī, and śatāvarī. (Ras 10.40)
In grain-vinegar (dhānyāmla), one should throw everything in after stirring it well, excluding the husks;
having been macerated for eleven times in this vinegar, [the substance] is processed with sixteen parts [of other ingredients]. (Rasāyana 10.41)
O Goddess, one should steam [the mercury] in a dolāyantra for three days over a gentle fire, using *āsuri*, salt, *vyoṣa*, *citraka*, ginger, and radish roots. (Rasāyana 10.42)
Aṅkola destroys poison, O beloved, while Āragvadha increases the digestive fire;
Citraka destroys impurities, and Kumārī removes the seven sheaths. (Rasāyana 10.43)
Therefore, the wise one should grind [the substance] with these combined together and cause it to fall [into the crucible]. (Rasāyana 10.44)

O Goddess, one should purify the mercury free from defects by means of the *vidyādhara* instrument; thereafter, that mercury, having been strained, should be placed upon a triple-layered cloth. (Rasārṇava 10.45)

One should grind it with *triphalā*, the root of *vahni*, and the juice of *gṛhakanyā* upon a stone that does not emit steam, and then subject it to the process of sublimation (*pātana*) again. (Rasāyana 10.46)
Then, one should grind [the mercury] for three days with the essence of *dhūma*, jaggery, *vyoṣa*, turmeric, white mustard seeds, brick, *kāñjika* sour gruel, and *ūrṇā*. (Rasārṇava 10.47)
The mercury becomes stainless and shall manifest my power. (Rasārṇava 10.48)
One should rub it with *vāsaka* and *vibhītaka* and cause it to fall [into a crucible] again;
thus, defects such as those arising from lead (*nāga*) and tin (*vaṅga*), as well as those produced by external impurities, go to destruction. (Rasāyana 10.49)
One should rub the mercury, which has had its defects removed, seven times with *kākamācī*;
by dropping it seven times [into water], the mercury will abandon the defect of mountain-ore. (Rasāyana 10.50)
O Goddess, one who has been intensified by the essence of *gokarṇa* should abandon the defects of the field. (Rasārṇava 10.51)
Steeped in the exudation of cotton leaves mixed with the three pungents (trikaṭuka) and stripped of its seven coats, the mercury is produced in seven days. (Rasakalpa 10.52)
Kākamācī, jayā, brāhmī, gāṅgerī, raktacitraka, maṇḍūkī, mudgaparṇī, śṛṅgavera, and rasāṅkuśa. (Rasāyana 10.53)
Devadālī, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Kākajaṅghā, Śatāvarī, Kumārī, Bhṛṅgarāja, Nirguṇḍī, and Grīṣmasundara. (Rasāyanatantra 10.54)
Śūlinī, śūrpaparṇī, gojihvā, and kṣīrakañcuka—rubbed with their juices, [the mercury] should be precipitated; after seven such cycles, it becomes pure. (Rasārṇava 10.55)
Having made a paste with copper, one should cause it to fall [into the crucible] by means of upward sublimation (*ūrdhvapātana*);
having abandoned tin and lead, the mercury (*sūtaka*) becomes pure. (Rasāyana 10.56)
Having been ground with triphalā, śigru, rājikā, paṭu, and citraka, it should be placed in an upper vessel and cooked over heated stones below. (Rasāyana 10.57)
By the cessation of the lotus of emanation (*sṛṣṭyambuja*), the *rasa* will be essentially attained;
[this is achieved] through the combination of *karkoṭī*, *kañcukī*, *bimbī*, *sarpākṣī*, and the lotus. (Ras 10.58)
One should place the mercury in a fluxing agent; it shall become brilliant and pure.
Thus purified, the mercury is dried with one-eighth part of *bhadra*. (Rasārṇava 10.59)

O Goddess, by means of *kṣudrā*, sour substances, salt, alkali, earth, *bhṛṅga*, *uṣaṇa*, and *śigru*, combined with black mustard (*rājikā*) and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), and processed in *āranāla* for three days through sweating, the mercury becomes stimulated and becomes desirous of food. (Rasārṇava 10.60)
O Goddess of the Gods, tell me that regarding the seeds of *vyoma*, *sattva*, and so forth, for the digestion and purification of mercury; what else do you wish to hear? (Rasārṇava 10.61)
11 [Bālajāraṇa] The illustrious Goddess said:
"I have heard the characteristics and the purification of mercury."
O Bhairava, I desire to hear about *cāraṇa* and *jāraṇa*. (Rasārṇava 11.1)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
When the destruction of all sins has occurred, the digestion of mercury (*rasajāraṇā*) is attained;
upon attaining that, the very gnosis which is the cause of liberation is indeed obtained. (Rasārṇava 11.2)
O Goddess, for the practitioner, *jāraṇa* (digestion) is that which manifests liberation;
however, as long as the mercury (*sūta*) is not digested, there is no final beatitude. (Rasārṇava 11.3)
O Goddess, the mortar is the pedestal, and the mercury is said to be the linga;
its grinding is the prostration, and its consumption is prescribed as the worship. (Rasārṇava 11.4)
For as many days as the mercury remains heated and maintained within the fire, for that many thousands of yugas one is glorified in the world of Śiva. (Rasārṇava 11.5)
He who offers even a single day’s worth of mercury into the fire—his sins melt away, and he is not defiled even while performing [worldly] acts. (Rasārṇava 11.6)
Digestion (jāraṇā) is of two kinds: the digestion of the child (bālajāraṇā) and the digestion of the bound (baddhajāraṇā).
Among these, O Supreme Goddess, the digestion of the child shall first be described. (Rasārṇava 11.7)
First, one should cause the sky to digest; after that, all the essences (sarvasattva);
then purified honey, and immediately thereafter gold. (Rasāyana 11.8)
Having first liquefied that which is situated within the embryo, one should then liquefy the external flux;
one should whiten it with a white substance and color it red with a red substance. (Rasārṇava 11.9)
Having understood *sāraṇa* and *krāmaṇa*, one should then employ *vedha*.
Oṃ, homage to the immortal metal, arisen from the supreme nectar-essence; hūṃ svāhā! Ras_11.11 //
"O Blessed One, for the benefit of all sentient beings, I wish to perform the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*) with your permission; O Lord, please accept my morsel. (Ras_11.12)
"Perform it," said Śiva; this must indeed be accepted by one of sound intellect. (Ras 11.13)
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the supreme digestion (*jāraṇa*) of mercury by means of the void (*vyoma*);
it is of two kinds: the digestion of mercury by means of leaf-like mica (*pattrābhra*) and the digestion by means of the essence (*sattva*). (Rasārṇava 11.14)
The faceless, the with-face, and likewise the face-of-impregnation—each of these is threefold; I shall explain them in due order. (Rasādhya 11.15)
O Goddess, through contact with *vaikrānta* diamond or by the power of divine herbs, the mercury, having become mouthless, shall in an instant devour the sky. *Rasārṇava 11.16*.
In the work of gold, gold itself is the primary ingredient; in silver, silver should be the principal element.

O Goddess, a paste made from heated *khalva* and very fine, minute quantities of mica, ground with *amlavetasa*, jambīra, bījapūra, sour earth, and mercury, undergoes digestion; this is known as *samukhajāraṇā*. (Rasārṇava 11.18)
One should digest the three alkalis, the five salts, kākṣī, kāsīsa, sulphur, and mākṣika, combined with acidic liquids, in a copper vessel. (Rasārṇava 11.19)

And having caused this divine [substance] to be processed through distillation, the wise one should do so for the sake of digesting (*jāraṇa*) the *bījas* and especially the *vajras*. (Rasāyana 11.20)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should pour [the liquid] over that mercury or tin which has been processed a hundred times for the purpose of an elixir. (Rasārṇava 11.21)
By this, O Goddess, one should contemplate the entire substance of the *cāraṇa*;
the sky, having been processed with alkali and acid, is then processed with the first powder. (Rasārṇava 11.22)
Macerated with the juice of *tumburu* and a drop of water from the three worlds, it may be administered or processed by being roasted in a *puṭa* with the juice of *yavaciñcā*. (Rasārṇava 11.23)
Śatāvarī, gadā, rambhā, meghanādā, punarnavā, śigruka, and yavaciñcā—[the preparation] should be sequentially impregnated with the juices of these. (Rasakalpa 11.24)
The root of *hilamocā*, the root of *kauverī*, as well as *kadalī*, *musalī*, *śigru*, *tāmbūlī*, *vāṇa*, and *pīluka*. (Ras 11.25)
Alambuṣā, balā, kola, āsphoṭa, kharamañjarī, tumburu, or tiktaśāka— using the juice of any one of these,
combined with rājikā and vyoṣa, abhraka should be steamed for three days. (Rasārṇava 11.26)
Combined with green vitriol, alum, rock salt, and borax alkali, mercury moves instantly through the previously described method of sublimation. (Rasārṇava 11.27)
It quickly becomes a pill that bestows all accomplishments. (Rasāyana 11.28)

O Goddess, having taken sour gruel (dhānyāmla) combined with the group of acidic substances (amlavarga), one should boil that abhraka and then rub it with the milky sap of the snuhī plant. (Rasārṇava 11.29)
Then, using forest cow-dung alone, one should prepare a crucible known as the "pigeon" (kapota).
With the sap of plantain roots, the juice of radish tubers, kākamācī, mīnākṣī, apāmārga, and likewise munī; Ras_11.31.
One should administer one *puṭa* each with the juices of castor oil plant (*eraṇḍa*), fresh ginger (*ārdraka*), blue water lily (*meghanāda*), and *punarnavā*. (Rasakalpa 11.32)
One should cook it with *vajrī* milk using a swinging-pan apparatus (*dolāyantra*);
then, having dried it in the shade, one should combine it with sour chickpea water (*caṇakāmla*). (Rasārṇava 11.33)
One should add navasāra, kāsīsa, vacā, and likewise nimba, each in an amount equal to one-sixteenth part of the mica. Ras_11.34 //
O lady of excellent vows, having placed it in a copper vessel, one should rub it;
then, O Goddess, one should cause it to be digested nine times in an iron vessel. (Rasārṇava 11.35)
O Goddess of the Gods, having boiled the sour gruel (kāñjika) with chickpea vinegar (caṇakāmla) and juice over a gentle fire for half a watch (prahara), it will be produced. (Rasārṇava 11.36)

Having ground *vyoma* (mica) together with *sauvarcala* salt using the juices of *somavallī*, one should cause it to be subjected to three *puṭa* cycles very slowly over *haṃsapādī*. (Rasārṇava 11.37)
One should cause it to be soaked seven times with the juice of *somavallī* alone;
then, combined with that juice, one should cast it into an earthen vessel. (Rasārṇava 11.38)
One should rub the root of the *siteṣupuṅkhā* with cow’s milk;
then, one should apply its paste to mercury and to the "sky" (mica) situated above it. (Rasārṇava 11.39)
One should heat it with the heat of the sun; for a moment, it swallows [the mercury] face-down, and a paste quickly arises—there is no need for deliberation on this point. (Ras 11.40)
O Dear One, one should saturate *gagana* with the juice of *tilaparṇī*;
through rubbing, a *piṣṭī* is produced—of this there is no doubt. (Rasārṇava 11.41)
One should repeatedly saturate nāga with the exudate of *muṇḍī*;
having then soaked the mica (*abhraka*) with that, one should burn it repeatedly in a crucible (*puṭa*). (Ras 11.42)
The powder of sulphur and mica should be diligently washed seven times with each of the following: citraka, fresh ginger, and dry ginger. (Rasāyana 11.43)

The mercury, having been processed with the juice of *nāgaśuṇḍī*, milk, soot, *luṅga*, and sour gruel, should likewise be subjected to the swinging process (*dolāyantra*) with sixteen parts [of the other ingredients]. (Rasārṇava 11.44)
O Goddess, O Beloved, one should administer [the medicine] sixty-four times the dose, or thirty-two times,
or sixteen times, or eight times,
or four times, or twice, or in equal measure. Ras_11.45.
O Pārvatī, hear now about the digestion (jāraṇa) of the supreme sattva of bhraka. Ras_11.46 //

The sattva of the sky, combined with an equal portion of the sattva of the ore to be heated—O Goddess, when the mercury is treated in this manner, it becomes a "womb-dissolver" (garbhadrāvī). RAS 11.47.
O Goddess, one should cause *nāgābhra*, *vaṅgābhra*, *tīkṣṇābhra*, *bhāskarābhraka*, *tārābhra*, and *hemābhra* to be digested by means of *rasagarbha*. (Rasārṇava 11.48)
Through the yoga of the previous consecration, it flows into the womb by means of friction.
The first [portion] consists of sixty-four parts, the second of thirty-two parts, the third of sixteen parts, and the fourth is indeed eight parts. (Ras 11.50)
The fifth part is declared to be a fourth part [of the previous], and the sixth is two parts; a morsel of mercury and of mica endowed with sattva should be administered. (Rasārṇava 11.51)

O Goddess of the Gods, when the consumption [of the breath] reaches sixty-four parts, the mercury becomes a bearer of the staff; and in the second stage of the yoga of consumption, it is like a leech. (Rasāyana 11.52)
With a third morsel, it becomes like crow-dung;
with a fourth morsel, it becomes like whey. (Rasāyana 11.53)
In the fifth stage of practice, during the swallowing of food, it becomes like butter;
in the sixth, however, it is like a ball of cow dung—these are the signs of gradual digestion. (Rasāyana 11.54)

Having sprinkled it with sour gruel (kāñjika) one hundred times until it becomes red as the sky, one should cause it to circulate within the mortar along with the impregnation of copper (śulvavāsanā). (Rasārṇava 11.55)
Having rubbed gold and silver together in a mortar, one should place mercury therein;
with the addition of *kāsīsa* and *sindhu*, the mercury flows. (Rasārṇava 11.56)
Having rubbed gold and lead together, one should cause the juice to be added therein;
when combined with lead and gold, the iron (vyoma) becomes completely digested and liquefied.
This [elixir] quickly devours the impurities of mica through its very mouth. (Rasārṇava 11.57)

Having rubbed together silver and tin, one should add mercury to it; when combined with lead and gold, the iron (vyoma) becomes fully digested and liquefied. It moves through the mouth and is highly recommended for the work of silvering. (Rasārṇava 11.58)
One should diligently cause [the breath] to move through the sky (nabhas), whether with the mouth open or closed. // Ras_11.59 //

Having thus performed the threefold *cāraṇā* in the mercury for the liquefaction (*druti*) of the embryo, one should digest and sweat the mass through the three stages of transformation. (Rasārṇava 11.60)
Having been smeared with sharp sour substances, alkali, cow urine, and the milk of *snuhī*,
and bound on the outside with a cloth, it should be offered another morsel [of food] and then steamed over a gentle fire in alkaline water, fermented gruel, and oil. (Ras 11.61)
O Queen of the Gods, by this sequence, the mercury—having been extracted from the apparatus and placed in an iron vessel—is matured in three days. (Rasārṇava 11.62)
First, it should be washed with lukewarm *kāñjika* and strained through a cloth;
then, one should rub it in a vessel with the hand until it is comfortably warm and only a residue remains. (Rasāyana 11.63)
Pressed with a fourfold cloth, it becomes stainless.

When the mass has been strained through the process of filtration and has emerged from the pressing, it becomes the "bearer of the staff" (daṇḍadhārī), and likewise the juice is the "digested mass" (jīrṇagrāsa). (Rasārṇava 11.65)
While the medicine is undigested, one should cause it to digest, foment it, and likewise rub it;
by employing *vetasāmla*, once it is digested, one should administer a morsel (*grāsa*). (Rasārṇava 11.66)

Mercury should be rubbed with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) and heated after being mixed with sixteen parts each of brick-dust, jaggery, burnt wool, *rājī* (black mustard), rock salt, and soot. (Rasārṇava 11.67)
However, for the sake of purification, with every morsel again and again,
even one whose clouds have vanished and whose seeds have perished takes up the passions, becoming stainless.
By this sequence, four morsels should be moved on the swing;
thereafter, heating and binding should be performed in succession by means of the tortoise-press. (Rasārṇava 11.69)
Having added viḍa salt by one-eighth part both above and below, one should cause it to digest;
O Dear One, when the mercury has fully digested the mica, it becomes a hundredfold penetrator (śatavedhī). (Rasārṇava 11.70)
When doubled, it pierces a thousand; when tripled, it pierces ten thousand;
when quadrupled, it becomes a mercury that moves on earth, piercing a hundred thousand. (Rasāyanasāstra 11.71)
O Goddess, when it has been digested five times, the mercury becomes the lifespan of Brahmā;
when it has been digested six times, O Viṣṇu, the mercury becomes a penetrator of ten million leagues.
All the defects of mercury, however, are destroyed by abhraka processed six times; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (Rasāyana 11.73)
O beloved, when the sky [abhraka] has been digested six times in the king of juices, it then devours the metals and abandons its own gait. (Rasārṇava 11.74)
Fuming, crackling, leaping like a frog, trembling, and quivering—these are the five stages of the rasa. (Ras 11.75)
Then Kapila emits sparks that do not rise upward;
he remains motionless within the fire—this is the characteristic of one who has digested the sky. (Rasāyana 11.76)
A child should digest [the medicine] three times over; one in youth, four times;
and an old man, six times. Thus, each should perform the action separately according to their stage of life. (Ras 11.77)

The "child" [stage] pierces metals by means of leaf-coating; the "youthful" stage by means of the application of a paste; and the "old" stage, once it has been processed through digestion (*jārita*) or purification (*sārita*), pierces them. (Rasārṇava 11.78)
But the rasa of childhood, O Goddess, is not capable of alchemy;
the rasa of youth, O Goddess, is capable of protecting the body. (Ras 11.79)

The mercury in the state of old age which enters the body through iron—in its absence, one should provide the essence of magnetite (kāntaloha) in place of the essence of mica (abhraka). (Rasārṇava 11.80)
In the absence of the beloved [mercury], one should instead administer sharp iron;
by this sequential application, one shall digest all elemental essences. (Rasārṇava 11.81)
Even a single [atom] of gold, when combined with mercury, becomes golden in an instant;
beyond that, there is nothing superior among the primary or secondary metals. (Rasāyana 11.82)

By means of the previously described application of the yantra, one should cause the sulphur—either sixteen times [the weight of the mercury], or twelve times, or even six times—to be digested. (Rasārṇava 11.83)

Having taken the essence (sattva) of honey-gold, one should cause it to be digested by means of a quarter-part [of mercury]; thereafter, one should likewise liquefy all other essences within the womb of the mercury. (Rasārṇava 11.84)
There is friendship between gold and fire, as well as between gold and mercury;
yet there is enmity between fire and mercury, and through their respective friends, there is mutual friendship between them. (Rasārṇava 11.85)
Agnika, yavaciñcā, vasuhaṭṭa, and rāgiṇī—cooked by means of swinging and sweating, this is the supreme digestion of gold. (Rasārṇava 11.86)

Ash of *palāśa*, *apāmārga*, barley alkali (*yavakṣāra*), sour gruel (*kāñjika*), black salt (*sauvarcala*), iron sulfate (*kāsīsa*), sea salt (*sāmudra*), and likewise rock salt (*saindhava*). (Ras_11.87)
One should take equal parts of āsurī, ṭaṅkaṇa, navasāra, as well as karpūra and mākṣika. (Rasāyana 11.88)
O Goddess of gods, one should apply a coating to the crucible with the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*;
then, having added powdered *viḍa* salt, O beloved, one should digest the gold. (Rasārṇava 11.89)
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the process of digestion known as *bhūcara*. (Rasārṇava 11.90)
One should mix black, yellow, and red minerals with mica in copper and steel.
O beloved, when the sharp powder is twenty-two times [the quantity] in the crucible, one should then gradually mix in half as much gandhanāga. (Rasārṇava 11.92)
